The public-risk waterfall A closure estimate should distinguish direct work from project management, contingency and long- term obligations. It should then distinguish the estimated obligation from the funds legally accessible after default. The resulting shortfall is a potential public exposure, not automatically a realised fiscal cost. The size of the shortfall depends on the scenario, the enforceability of guarantees and the performance of remaining assets.

Independent cost estimate: Cost estimate prepared or challenged by qualified professionals separate from the operator’s production incentives. Mine relinquishment: Formal transfer or discharge of defined responsibilities after closure conditions are satisfied. Net present value: Discounted value of a sequence of future cash flows under stated assumptions. Post-closure: Period after cessation of closure works when monitoring, maintenance or treatment may continue. Progressive rehabilitation: Rehabilitation conducted while mine operations continue. Residual risk: Risk remaining after planned closure controls and works. Ring-fenced trust: Assets legally segregated for a defined purpose with trustee governance. Surety bond: Third-party commitment to respond to specified obligations under bond terms. Tailings: Residual material from mineral processing requiring safe storage and management. Third-party cost: Cost for an external contractor or authority to perform required works. Water rebound: Change in groundwater level after mine dewatering stops. Closing proposition Mining closure is not a peripheral obligation at the end of extraction. It is a test of whether the economic benefits of a finite activity are matched by durable responsibility for its consequences. The physical work, the accounting estimate, the financial instrument and the social transition must form one coherent system. The central public-interest question is practical: when a mine stops producing, who pays, who acts, who verifies, and what happens if the original assumptions fail? pages.text: RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / GLOBAL RESEARCH / OCTOBER 2026 THE WATER ALLOCATION ECONOMY | 1 GLOBAL RESEARCH MONOGRAPH | FLAGSHIP EDITION | 2026 THE WATER ALLOCATION ECONOMY Mining, AI Infrastructure, Hydrogen and the Next Constraint on Industrial Growth CORE THESIS The next industrial constraint is not simply the availability of freshwater. It is the ability to allocate dependable, lawful and ecologically credible water across competing uses while accounting for the electricity, infrastructure and social costs of supply. A global assessment of mining, digital infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing, hydrogen, energy systems, water reuse, industrial finance and basin governance. Ragunauth Ramsaroop 19 October 2026 Evidence reviewed through 19 October 2026. Quantitative statements distinguish observed data, forecasts, institutional assessments and author-developed scenarios.

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / GLOBAL RESEARCH / OCTOBER 2026 THE WATER ALLOCATION ECONOMY | 2 Executive Intelligence Water is becoming a binding industrial-location and investment variable. The constraint is rarely captured by the headline price of water. A project needs supply in the right place, at the right quality, during the right season, under enforceable rights, and with infrastructure able to deliver through adverse conditions. In a stressed basin, those requirements connect corporate strategy with public services, ecosystem health and social legitimacy. This paper treats water as a shared economic system rather than an isolated operational input. The 2026 United Nations water assessment reports 2.1 billion people without safely managed drinking water. World Resources Institute analysis identifies 25 countries, containing about one- quarter of the global population, under extremely high annual water stress. The United Nations reports that agriculture accounted for 72% of global freshwater withdrawals in the referenced 2022 data, industry 15% and services 13%. These figures describe different dimensions of risk and should not be combined into a single scarcity index. [01] [02] [03] New industrial demands complicate the allocation problem. Data centres need cooling and electricity. Semiconductor manufacturing needs high-purity water. Mines need process water and safe tailings management. Green hydrogen needs treated water, while desalination and pumping consume energy. The result is a set of linked constraints rather than a single volume shortage. The IEA projects data-centre electricity consumption around 945 TWh in 2030 in its 2025 Base Case, but electricity growth alone does not determine site-level water consumption. RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / GLOBAL RESEARCH / OCTOBER 2026 THE WATER ALLOCATION ECONOMY | 5 Methodology and Evidence Discipline The research uses a mixed strategic synthesis rather than an econometric causal model. The source hierarchy gives preference to current official data, international institutions, national technical agencies, peer-reviewed scholarship and standards organisations. The analysis compares published evidence with explicit conceptual propositions. It does not treat an announced policy or a modelled scenario as an observed result. Primary-source data are not mechanically harmonised. The UN freshwater-withdrawal shares refer to a specified reporting year. WRI Aqueduct is a modelled screening system. Cochilco operational results refer to the Chilean copper sector, while its 2034 figures are projections. LBNL data-centre figures combine historical estimates and future scenarios. Their definitions and time periods remain visible. Scholarly discovery includes the 2025 LBNL workload water-use review, the systematic literature review of reuse barriers, and research on mining-related public water concerns. Scholarly publications help challenge assumptions but do not automatically override directly observed local hydrology or legal requirements. [28] [29] [30] The study avoids a universal litres-per-unit benchmark across unrelated processes. An industrial water metric is meaningful only when its boundary, location, timing, quality and production denominator are defined. Similarly, a country-level stress score is useful for screening but insufficient for a permit or investment decision. The Allocation Question Water scarcity becomes an industrial constraint when a project has nominal access to water but lacks reliable, lawful and socially acceptable supply through its full operating life. A credible investment appraisal must distinguish basin availability, legal entitlement, seasonal deliverability, quality, treatment requirements and competing uses. Annual national water balances obscure the months and subcatchments where operations fail. The recurrent failure is to treat water as a purchased input whose tariff represents its full economic cost. The tariff often excludes system expansion, drought exposure, ecosystem damage, political legitimacy and third-party effects. Boards should require a basin-adjusted water supply plan alongside power, logistics and financial models. Governments should require comparable disclosures without treating private contractual arrangements as substitutes for public allocation decisions. Analytical boundary. The question is not resolved by a single indicator. The Energy-Water Feedback Water and energy are coupled through cooling, pumping, treatment, desalination, hydropower and thermal generation. The effect of dry cooling, desalination, hydrogen electrolysis, water reuse and industrial recycling depends on electricity source, ambient climate, process design, water quality, geography and scale. The BASIN framework and control library are original analytical tools without external certification or statistical validation. RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / GLOBAL RESEARCH / OCTOBER 2026 THE WATER ALLOCATION ECONOMY | 158 Closing Proposition The next industrial bottleneck is not a simple contest over how many cubic metres a project can purchase. It is the capacity to reconcile physical water, lawful allocation, dependable infrastructure, industrial productivity, public services and ecosystem limits within the same decision. A water- efficient facility can still be a poor basin investment. A water-intensive facility can become more resilient when its demand finances verified reuse, treatment and shared infrastructure without shifting costs to others. The strategic task for boards and institutions is to move from isolated water-volume targets to an integrated allocation discipline. Measure the basin, respect rights, test supply, price the full system, protect nature and verify outcomes. Industrial growth will be more durable when its water assumptions are as transparent and stress-tested as its financial assumptions. Ragunauth Ramsaroop | 19 October 2026

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | THE CARBON INTEGRITY DIVIDE | 3 EXECUTIVE INTELLIGENCE Executive thesis Carbon markets are entering a phase in which the legal meaning of a tonne matters as much as its price. A tonne reported in a corporate inventory is not automatically a transferable credit. A credit retired in a voluntary registry is not automatically an internationally transferred mitigation outcome. A product footprint is not a national inventory. A border-adjustment certificate is not an offset. These distinctions are now operational questions for boards, exporters, project developers, governments and assurance providers. [01][03][10][14] The paper argues for a shift from single-number carbon narratives to reconciled, evidence-bearing claims. A credible climate statement should identify its physical boundary, the intervention that produced a change, the registry and legal status of any unit, the national accounting treatment, the product or corporate reporting treatment, and the precise public claim. The absence of any one layer does not necessarily invalidate all climate action. It does limit what a buyer or issuer can assert. This is the organising proposition of the Seven-Ledger Integrity Architecture, introduced here as original author analysis. Three developments make the issue urgent. The World Bank reports 87 direct carbon-pricing policies and coverage of just over 29 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions in its 2026 assessment. The UNFCCC approved the first Article 6.4 issuance in February 2026 and expanded eligible methodology coverage during the year. The EU CBAM definitive regime began in January 2026, while new corporate accounting and claims standards continued to evolve. [01][03][04][10][14][16] The World Bank reports more than US$107 billion in carbon-pri

A board-level decision model distinguishing a compliance obligation, a mitigation investment, a carbon credit, a product footprint and a reputational claim. Why a tonne is not a single financial instrument The same physical reduction can be described in several systems without becoming interchangeable across them. Procurement teams should record whether a unit is being acquired for legal surrender, CORSIA cancellation, voluntary contribution, corporate target implementation or another defined purpose. The size and shape of carbon pricing in 2026 The World Bank reports 87 carbon-pricing policies, average direct carbon prices near US$21 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent and just over 29 percent global emissions coverage in its 2026 review. Revenue exceeded US$107 billion in 2025. These are different indicators: policy count, price, coverage and revenue. None by itself measures the quantity of additional mitigation caused by pricing. [01][02] A carbon tax fixes a price and allows emissions quantities to respond. An emissions trading system constrains or manages allowance supply and permits prices to respond. Both systems can include exemptions, free allo

Physical emissions inventories and the accounting boundary The greenhouse-gas inventory is the foundation of credible corporate climate management. Scope 1 covers direct sources controlled or owned by the organisation under the chosen consolidation approach. Scope 2 addresses emissions associated with purchased energy. Scope 3 addresses other value-chain categories. The specific rules and disclosures depend on the applicable standard and reporting programme. [14][15][27] An inventory should specify the organisational boundary, facilities, consolidation method, reporting period, gas coverage, emission factors, activity data, calculation methods and recalculation policy. Without these fields, apparent annual progress may reflect acquisitions, divestments, changed factors or boundary shifts rather than operational decarbonisation. Physical inventory totals should remain distinguishable from market-based contractual reporting and from claimed impacts of separate actions. The GHG Protocol announced in July 2026 a future consolidated standard with ISO, targeted for publication in the fourth quarter of 2028. Its interim discussion of multi-statement reporting emphasises separation rather than indiscriminate netting. [14] For a mining group, physical emissions include fuel combustion, process emissions where relevant and purchased electricity. Supplier emissions and product use may fall into Scope 3 categories depending on the business. A low-carbon certificate or credit does not era

Hourly matching may improve temporal specificity but increases data requirements and can alter procurement cost and feasibility. An effective control system preserves meter readings, generation certificates, retirement records, market boundaries and the time interval of matching. Claims should name the reporting method. A phrase such as renewable-powered can conceal important differences between onsite generation, direct wire, contracted supply and annual attribute procurement. The analytical test is to distinguish three statements: what the facility consumed physically, which attributes it acquired contractually, and what system-level emissions impact its investment produced. These are related but not interchangeable statements. Additionality as a financing and causal question Additionality concerns whether an intervention delivers mitigation beyond the relevant baseline and would have occurred without the crediting incentive or under prevailing requirements. Different methodologies use financial, barrier, common-practice, regulatory or performance tests. No single test is equally informative in every sector. [06][19][20] In an industrial project, the additionality question often centres on the investment decision. A waste- heat recovery system may save energy and money without credit revenue. A methane-abatement project may be financially unattractive absent credit income. A new renewable plant may be built for commercial reasons unrelated to carbon finance. Each requires project-specific evidence. The most informative record is contemporaneous. Investment committee papers, alternative project evaluations, financing conditions, tariff assumptions and regulatory obligations are stronger evidence than retrospective statements. A claimed financial barrier should be consistent with the project model and with actual investment behaviour. For buyers, additionality due diligence should distinguish programme approval from project-level evidence. The ICVCM Core Carbon Principles provide a programme and methodology quality threshold. They do not replace scrutiny of the unit vintage, project, issuance record and intended c

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | THE CARBON INTEGRITY DIVIDE | 9 analysis and market effects. Energy projects may require dispatch modelling. A universal leakage discount is rarely a substitute for a relevant causal model. Corporate inventories and project crediting handle displacement differently. A company may report a reduction within its own boundary while emissions rise elsewhere in the value chain. A crediting project may need to deduct leakage under its methodology. Neither result alone establishes the net global effect of the intervention. The control response is a leakage register with a named mechanism, geographic scope, monitoring variable, expected direction, uncertainty range and escalation trigger. Buyers should examine whether the leakage treatment remains credible when the project scales. Article 6.2 and sovereign accounting Article 6.2 enables cooperative approaches involving internationally transferred mitigation outcomes under agreed accounting and reporting arrangements. Host-country authorisation, first transfer, corresponding adjustments and reporting status are separate matters. The UNFCCC publishes initial and regular information reports and technical-review status for participating Parties. [32] A host country may have reasons to retain mitigation for its own nationally determined contribution rather than authorise export. The economic value of an authorised unit should therefore be assessed alongside the opportunity cost of adjusting the host-country account. The correct policy balance depends on national targets, marginal abatement costs and development priorities. The buyer should examine the exact authorisation instrument, permitted use, vintages, quantities, transfer conditions, revocation provisions and corresponding-adjustment arrangements. A press announcement or memorandum of understanding is not a substitute for the required accounting and legal evidence. The Seven-Ledger framework treats sovereign accounting as an independent ledger. A registry retirement records unit use. A national corresponding adjustment addresses double claiming between participating countries. Neither operation should be inferred from the other without evidence. Analytical test R

Projects need a methodology, host-country participation conditions, registration, monitoring, verification, issuance and any required authorisation for intended use. Timelines and project risk differ at each stage. The analysis therefore treats Article 6.4 as a developing institutional architecture. Claims about market scale, credit volume or future finance flows should be described as forecasts or aspirations unless supported by actual issued and transacted units. Registry infrastructure and chain of title A registry records units, serial numbers, project identities, issuance, transfers, cancellations and retirement status according to programme rules. A registry is essential for traceability, but a unique serial number alone does not prove environmental additionality or legal suitability for every purpose. [19][20]

Corporate claims and the meaning of contribution A company can finance mitigation outside its value chain without reducing its reported physical inventory by the same amount. The distinction between an emissions-reduction claim, a carbon- neutrality claim and a contribution claim is central to credible communication. VCMI updated its Claims Code to version 3.2 in September 2026, while ISO 14068:2026 established a hierarchy prioritising reductions and removals within the value chain before offsetting residual footprints. [18] [22][23] A defensible claim should state the boundary, period, standard, emissions trend, credits used, project type, unit status and whether the claim concerns compensation, contribution or achievement of a target. The marketing language should not exceed what the accounting evidence supports. The risk is especially acute for product labels. Consumers may interpret carbon neutral as meaning a product has negligible lifecycle emissions when the claim depends on external credits. EU Directive 2024/825 specifically addresses product claims based on greenhouse-gas offsetting, with application from September 2026. [11][12] A claims committee should include legal, technical, sustainability and commercial representation. Approval should be linked to a controlled claims register. The GHG Protocol-ISO convergence In July 2026 the GHG Protocol announced a joint corporate standard-development programme with ISO. The published target is a consolidated public consultation in the second quarter of 2027 and a joint standard in the fourth quarter of 2028. This is a development timetable, not a currently effective replacement for all existing reporting requirements. [14][15] The convergence responds to a persistent reporting problem: different frameworks may use different boundaries, terminology and recognition rules. Harmonisation can reduce duplicated work, but it also requires organisations to maintain clear version control during transition. Companies should preserve raw activity data and method assumptions rather than storing only annual totals. This makes recalculation possible if consolidation approaches, emission factors or Scope 2 treatment change. A transition plan should specify the owner of each standard and the date on which reporting policies are updated. The Seven-Ledger architecture is designed to be standard-neutral. It does not assert that a future standard will adopt its structure. Its purpose is to prevent premature netting and to keep different evidence types recoverable. Aviation, CORSIA and purpose-specific eligibility ICAO maintains criteria and lists of emissions-unit programmes eligible for use under CORSIA. Programme approval is tied to specific compliance periods, vintages and conditions. ICAO reported eight approved programmes for the 2024-2026 first phase in a November 2025 update, while later assessment cycles continue. [24][25][39] CORSIA eligibility is not equivalent to generic voluntary-market eligibility. An airline needs units meeting the relevant compliance-period conditions and must cancel the required quantity. Host- country authorisation and avoidance of double claiming are material in specified cases. A procurement contract should specify the CORSIA phase, eligible programme, project type, vintage, authorisation evidence, corresponding-adjustment status, delivery deadline and remedy for ineligibility. A credit suited to a voluntary contribution claim may not be eligible for aviation compliance, a domestic scheme or an international transfer. papers.title: The Chokepoint Economy: Critical Minerals, Export Controls and the New Architecture of Industrial Security

pages.text: RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 1 GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 21 SEPTEMBER 2026 THE CHOKEPOINT ECONOMY Critical Minerals, Export Controls and the New Architecture of Industrial Security THESIS The strategic contest over critical minerals has moved beyond access to ore. The decisive risks now sit at processing chokepoints, trade controls, qualification standards, finance and industrial capacity. Governments and companies that measure security only by mine supply will misdiagnose the problem. Ragunauth Ramsaroop Independent global thought leadership on resources, industrial policy, economic security and responsible development.

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 2 Executive Summary The critical-minerals debate has entered a new phase. Supply concentration is still high, but concentration alone no longer describes the risk. Export controls, quotas, licensing regimes, industrial-policy conditions and qualification bottlenecks now determine whether physical material becomes usable industrial supply. The International Energy Agency reports that refining concentration across key energy minerals reached a new high in 2025. The average share held by the leading refining country rose to 70%, and to 72% when rare earths are excluded. For gallium, graphite, manganese and rare earths, the leading refiner, China, accounts for more than 90% of global supply. The IEA also reports that investment in critical-mineral development fell 9% in 2025 after several years of growth. The OECD's 2026 inventory shows a parallel change in trade policy. Export restrictions on critical raw materials are five times higher than in 2009. Across 2022-2024, about 16% of global trade in monitored critical raw materials faced at least one export restriction. Exposure reached about 67% for cobalt, 66% for manganese, 47% for natural graphite and 45% for rare earth elements. The policy response is becoming more interventionist. The European Union is using strategic-project designation and a Raw Materials Mechanism to connect buyers, suppliers, finance and storage. The United States has directed greater domestic and allied sourcing for defence supply chains and has expanded authorities linked to critical-material security. Producer countries are also using quotas, licensing and other restrictions to retain more value at home. This paper argues that the next stage of mineral security should be governed through a five-

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 3 1. The Risk Has Moved Downstream For much of the last decade, critical-mineral strategy focused on geological access. That was necessary, but it is no longer sufficient. The most consequential vulnerabilities increasingly sit between the mine and the factory. The IEA's 2026 outlook records higher refining concentration in 2025 than in 2023. Indonesia dominates nickel refining, while China is the leading refiner for most other major energy minerals. The top refining country averaged 70% of supply in 2025. Excluding rare earths, the figure was 72%. In gallium, graphite, manganese and rare earths, China accounts for more than 90% of refined supply. This matters because a mine does not automatically create industrial independence. Ore must be separated, purified, converted into chemicals, metals or components, certified against technical specifications, transported under stable trade rules and integrated into manufacturing systems. Each step creates a possible chokepoint. The United States made the same distinction explicit in its January 2026 action on processed critical minerals and derivative products. The policy finding stated that domestic mining does not secure supply when downstream processing remains dependent on foreign capacity. That is a useful analytical principle even outside the US policy context. Verified fact IEA data show refining concentration reached new highs in 2025, while investment in critical-mineral development fell 9% in the same year. Author analysis The strategic unit of analysis should shift from the mine to the complete industrial chain. Mineral security is a systems problem. 2. Export Controls Have Become an Industrial Variable Trade policy now changes mineral availability almost as quickly

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 4 3. The SPRQR Framework Source Measure mining concentration, ownership, permitting risk, water and power dependence, social licence, fiscal stability and project maturity. A resource estimate is not equivalent to dependable supply. Process Map refining, separation, precursor, metal and component capacity. Identify proprietary technology, reagent, equipment and skilled-labour dependencies. Processing is often more concentrated than extraction. Route Map export licences, quotas, tariffs, sanctions exposure, customs routes, shipping nodes and bilateral agreements. The route layer converts policy decisions into physical availability. Qualify Measure the time and technical burden required for a new source to enter aerospace, defence, automotive, semiconductor, battery or grid applications. A diversified supplier base on paper is not resilient if buyers have not qualified the alternatives. Recycle Measure collection rates, scrap access, recovery yields, economics, refining capacity and product standards. Secondary material becomes strategic supply only after a functioning reverse chain exists. 4. Three Policy Models Are Emerging Model A: Strategic autonomy Model B: Domestic and allied security Model C: Resource-based industrialisation Policy tension Consumer economies want open, diversified supply. Producer economies want greater domestic value capture. Durable mineral partnerships need to reconcile both objectives through investment, infrastructure, skills, technology transfer, transparent fiscal terms and credible long-term offtake.

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 5 5. Why Diversification Is Harder Than Announcing a New Mine New mining capacity faces long development timelines, but the less visible constraint is qualification. Industrial buyers cannot substitute critical inputs instantly. Chemical purity, particle size, magnetic performance, thermal behaviour, reliability, traceability and manufacturing compatibility all matter. The IEA's 2026 outlook highlights limited substitution options for several high-risk materials and notes that many are co-products or by-products. Gallium, for example, is mainly recovered alongside aluminium and zinc-related production. Tellurium is linked to copper and lead processing. Germanium is linked to zinc and coal. Supply therefore does not always respond cleanly to higher prices. This creates a policy trap. Governments often announce diversification targets in tonnes, while manufacturers experience security in qualified, specification-compliant material. The difference between the two is industrial readiness. 6. Finance Is Now Part of Security Policy Critical-mineral projects compete against incumbent supply chains with established infrastructure, customer relationships and cost advantages. Price volatility weakens investment signals. The IEA reports that critical-mineral investment fell 9% in 2025, ending several years of growth. Public policy is responding through strategic-project status, concessional finance, guarantees, demand aggregation, stockpiles and procurement preferences. These tools address a real market failure: private investors hesitate to fund high-cost alternative capacity when dominant suppliers can expand rapidly or when prices fall before projects reach production. The discipline required is to avoid converting security po

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 6 8. Policy Recommendations 1. Measure chokepoints, not only reserves. Publish supply-chain maps across mining, refining, trade routes, qualification and recycling. Geological abundance should not be used as a proxy for security. 2. Build qualification capacity into industrial policy. Fund testing laboratories, standards alignment, certification and accelerated buyer qualification alongside new mining and refining projects. 3. Use public finance to crowd in resilience. Tie guarantees, loans and strategic-project support to clear milestones, private capital participation, cost discipline and environmental and social performance. 4. Pair producer-country value addition with infrastructure. Domestic-processing goals need reliable power, water, transport, skills, finance and customer access. Export restrictions without these conditions risk reducing investment rather than building industry. 5. Create reciprocal mineral partnerships. Consumer economies should offer bankable offtake, finance, technology and skills. Producer economies should offer transparent rules, stable access and credible project execution. 6. Treat recycling as industrial capacity. Move beyond recycling targets. Build collection systems, processing capacity, product standards and offtake for secondary materials. 7. Stress-test corporate supply chains. Boards should test scenarios involving export controls, sanctions, shipping disruption, dominant-refiner outages and delayed qualification of alternative suppliers. 8. Protect openness where possible. Strategic security and open trade are not mutually exclusive. Transparency, predictable licensing and narrower measures reduce the risk that resilience policy fragments markets further. 9. Implementation Logic

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 7 Assessments of supply risk, market concentration and policy effects are attributed to the institutions that published them. Author propositions The SPRQR Framework, board-risk approach, reciprocal mineral partnership model and 12-month resilience review are the author's analytical proposals. Scope limit This paper addresses global industrial and economic-security architecture. It does not assess any individual company's confidential supply chain, any specific investment security, or the legal validity of a particular trade measure.

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | GLOBAL STRATEGY WHITE PAPER | 8 11. Scrutiny Audit IEA concentration figures were checked against the Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 executive summary, market overview and outlook sections. OECD trade-restriction figures were checked against the 2026 Inventory of Export Restrictions on Critical Raw Materials, published 28 April 2026. The OECD dataset covers measures through the end of 2024. Later policy examples are sourced separately and are not presented as part of the OECD 2024 inventory. The IEA's US$6.5 trillion figure is labelled as an estimate of annual downstream production outside China exposed under full implementation of expanded rare-earth controls. It is not described as a forecast loss. The EU Raw Materials Mechanism launch date, purpose and 17-material scope were checked against European Commission material published in April 2026. The US July 2026 defence-supply-chain action is described by its operative sourcing, mapping and qualification provisions. Political promotional language from the source is excluded. No claim is made that export restrictions are uniformly harmful. The paper distinguishes producer-country development objectives from execution and market-fragmentation risks. No claim is made that national self-sufficiency is necessary or economically optimal. The paper argues for system resilience through diversification and redundancy. All monetary figures use the currency stated in the source. No currency conversion is required for the core analysis. 12. References 1. International Energy Agency. papers.title: AI Assurance for Guyana's Extractive Sector: A Risk-Based Governance Blueprint for Mining, Environmental Compliance and Worker Protection

pages.text: AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 1 INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER AI Assurance for Guyana's Extractive Sector A risk-based governance blueprint for mining, environmental compliance and worker protection Core thesis. Guyana should allow AI adoption in mining to advance quickly, while requiring stronger assurance as the consequence of an AI-supported decision rises. The governing principle should be simple: no algorithm should weaken legal accountability, environmental evidence, worker rights, or the duty of a named human decision-maker. Prepared by Ragunauth Ramsaroop Georgetown, Guyana | 14 September 2026 Evidence cut-off: 14 September 2026. All time-sensitive claims were checked against sources available by this date.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 2 Executive Summary Guyana is moving toward a more digital state at the same time that its extractive industries are expanding. Budget 2026 identifies AskGov, the MyGuyana Citizen Portal and the e-ID system as core digital initiatives. In November 2025, the Government and Cerebras Systems announced a memorandum of understanding for an AI data centre of up to 100 MW at Wales. These developments show national intent to build digital capacity, but they do not by themselves create a governance regime for AI used in mines, regulators, workplaces or environmental decision-making. Mining is a strong candidate for early AI adoption because the sector combines large data flows with costly equipment, complex processing, remote operations, environmental obligations and safety-critical decisions. Global operators already report AI use in plant control, computer vision, predictive maintenance, digital twins, hazard reporting and automation. BHP reports that AI- powered plant control at Escondida has saved 3 billion litres of water and 118 GWh of energy [16] since FY2022. This is a company-reported result and should be treated as attributed evidence rather than an independently verified benchmark. The policy issue is therefore not whether AI belongs in mining. The issue is how Guyana preserves accountability when an AI system influences a blast plan, a worker-risk alert, a tailings decision, an environmental anomaly, an ore estimate, a procurement screen or a regulatory recommendation. Existing mining and environmental rules continue to assign duties to licence holders, agencies and people. AI should strengthen those duties, not blur them. This paper proposes a Guyana Extractive AI Assurance Framework

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 3 Five decisions that matter now 1 Issue sector guidance before high- consequence deployment GGMC, EPA and the Ministry of Labour should define minimum AI assurance expectations for mining and mineral processing. 2 Classify by consequence, not by model type A simple spreadsheet model that influences a tailings response may deserve more scrutiny than a large language model used for drafting. 3 Keep a named human accountable Every material AI-supported decision should retain an identified person with authority to accept, reject or stop the output. 4 Require evidence trails Data sources, model versions, key inputs, validation results and material decisions should be logged and retrievable. 5 Build local capability with industry A small regulatory AI assurance unit, supported by universities and operators, should develop sector competence before rules become more prescriptive.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 4 1. Why this question belongs on Guyana's agenda now Guyana's policy setting has shifted quickly. The 2026 Budget projects 17.6 percent growth in mining and quarrying [1], with gold and bauxite projected to expand by 5.4 percent and 19.3 percent respectively. The 2026 Budget Speech estimates that mining and quarrying expanded by 21 percent in 2025 [2] and that gold declarations reached 484,321 ounces [2]. These are government estimates and projections, not final audited national accounts. The same state is investing in digital public infrastructure. Budget 2026 lists AskGov, the MyGuyana Citizen Portal and e-ID-linked services among the planned digitalisation measures. A September 2026 government release continued to describe digital transformation, connectivity and domestic innovation as national priorities. Separately, the Government and Cerebras Systems announced an MOU in November 2025 for an AI data centre of up to 100 MW in Wales [9][10]. The project should be described as an announced partnership, not as an operating facility. This combination matters. A growing extractive sector, expanding digital infrastructure and a state that is openly adopting AI create a short policy window. Rules written after a technology becomes embedded are harder to enforce, and governance added after an incident tends to be more costly than governance designed into procurement, operating procedures and permits. What existing Guyanese rules already imply Mining regulation already assumes identifiable responsibility. GGMC's published process for a mining licence requires technical and financial capability, a work programme and an EPA environmental permit before a licence is issued. Medium-scale permits a

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 5 Evidence status used in this paper VERIFIED FACT Directly supported by legislation, an official government publication, an international standard body, or another primary source. ATTRIBUTED CLAIM Reported by a company, minister, institution or project sponsor. The attribution is retained. PROJECTION Forward estimate, target, planned project or announced timetable. It is not presented as a completed outcome. POLICY PROPOSITION Author recommendation or analytical judgement. It is separated from factual description.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 6 2. Where AI creates value, and where it creates exposure The strongest case for AI in mining is not novelty. It is the ability to combine sensor data, operating history, images, maintenance records and process variables at a speed that supports earlier action. Global mining examples already cover the full value chain. Use area Potential value Primary governance exposure Exploration and geology Target generation, core logging support, geospatial pattern detection Model bias can steer capital toward false positives or underweight local geological knowledge. Mine planning and processing Grade prediction, plant optimisation, recovery forecasting, digital twins Poor data or model drift can affect production, energy, reagent use and reserve confidence. Mobile equipment and autonomy Collision avoidance, autonomous haulage, remote operation Failures can create direct physical safety consequences. Maintenance Failure prediction, condition monitoring, computer vision False negatives can defer maintenance. False positives can waste scarce parts and labour. Environment and ESG Water, emissions, biodiversity and land-disturbance monitoring Models can miss anomalies or create false confidence if sensors, baselines or thresholds are weak. Workforce and safety Hazard reporting, fatigue detection, access control, scheduling Worker privacy, unfair profiling, surveillance and opaque employment decisions become material risks. Compliance and permitting Document screening, anomaly detection, inspection prioritisation Automated recommendations can bias regulatory attention or conceal the reasoning behind a decision. Supply chain and procurement Vendor risk, fraud flags, demand forecasting Poor data can unfai

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 7 What global practice already shows BHP stated in May 2025 that AI-powered plant control at Escondida had saved 3 billion litres of water and 118 GWh of energy [16] since FY2022. In January 2026, BHP also described computer- vision monitoring of conveyors and rail-loading systems and a voice-to-text hazard reporting application linked to historical incident data. These examples show potential operational value, while also illustrating why data quality, alert thresholds, override logic and accountability need formal controls. The ILO's 2025 global report [15] on AI and digitalisation at work reaches a balanced conclusion. Automation and intelligent monitoring can reduce hazardous exposures and support prevention, but new risks require proactive, evidence-informed and participatory policy responses. For mining, worker involvement is especially important where AI affects fatigue monitoring, productivity scoring, scheduling, access control or disciplinary decisions.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 8 3. A four-tier risk model for extractive AI The proposed model classifies an AI use by consequence rather than by technical sophistication. The test is not whether a system uses machine learning, generative AI or computer vision. The test is what happens when the system is wrong, unavailable, manipulated or misunderstood. Tier Consequence Examples Minimum control Tier 1 Low consequence Drafting, translation, routine analytics, non- binding summaries Owner approval, basic data controls, usage log, confidentiality rules. Tier 2 Material operational Predictive maintenance, process optimisation, geospatial targeting, supplier risk support Validation dataset, performance thresholds, drift monitoring, change control, named owner. Tier 3 High consequence Autonomous equipment, safety alerts, environmental compliance signals, worker scoring, permit recommendations Independent validation, human decision gate, fail-safe mode, incident reporting, auditable logs, periodic assurance. Tier 4 Restricted / exceptional Fully automated enforcement, unreviewed dismissal decisions, autonomous override of critical safety controls, irreversible regulatory action without accountable human review Do not deploy unless legislation, due process, technical assurance and competent authority explicitly support the use. Table 2. Proposed risk tiers. Policy proposition by the author.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 9 The consequence test • Physical safety: Could a wrong output expose a person to injury or remove a safety barrier? • Environmental consequence: Could a wrong output delay detection of pollution, land disturbance, water stress or tailings risk? • Rights and employment: Could the output affect hiring, discipline, termination, surveillance or access to benefits? • Regulatory consequence: Could the output influence whether a permit, sanction, inspection or enforcement action occurs? • Financial materiality: Could the output materially affect reserve reporting, production commitments, procurement or public revenue? • Reversibility: Is the decision easy to reverse, or does a wrong decision create lasting harm?

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 10 4. The Guyana Extractive AI Assurance Framework The framework below draws on ISO/IEC 42001 [11], the OECD AI Principles [12] and NIST AI RMF, then adapts those concepts to the operating reality of mines and regulators. ISO/IEC 42001 [11] provides a management-system structure for responsible AI. The OECD principles emphasise human oversight, transparency, robustness, safety and accountability. NIST organises practical risk management around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. 1. Consequence classification Every AI use receives a tier before deployment. Reclassification occurs when the use, data or decision authority changes. 2. Named human accountability A responsible person owns the use case and has authority to reject, stop or override AI- supported decisions. 3. Data provenance and integrity Material data sources, ownership, quality checks, transformations and retention rules are documented. 4. Testing, monitoring and change control Performance is tested before deployment, monitored after deployment and revalidated after material changes. 5. Explainability and contestability Affected people and regulators receive enough information to understand the role of AI and challenge material outcomes where appropriate. 6. Incident response and assurance Material failures, near misses, data breaches and unsafe outputs trigger defined escalation, evidence preservation and review. Figure 1. Six-pillar assurance model. Policy proposition by the author. Minimum evidence pack for Tier 3 systems • System purpose, decision boundary and prohibited uses. • Named accountable owner and named technical custodian. • Data inventory, provenance record and access controls. • Validation plan, test results, known

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 11 5. How Guyana can govern without slowing responsible innovation A new standalone AI regulator is not the first requirement for extractives. The first requirement is coordinated competence inside institutions that already hold mining, environmental, labour, data and standards mandates. A sector protocol can begin as guidance, procurement requirements and permit-linked expectations, then mature as evidence accumulates. Institution / actor Proposed role GGMC Lead sector inventory of AI uses in mining. Embed assurance expectations in technical reviews, inspection protocols and guidance for licence holders. EPA Set expectations for AI used in environmental monitoring, EIA support, emissions, water, biodiversity and compliance evidence. Require traceable human sign-off for material conclusions. Ministry of Labour and Manpower Planning Address worker monitoring, algorithmic management, occupational safety and consultation. Preserve worker voice where AI affects working conditions. GNBS Support standards alignment, including awareness of ISO/IEC 42001 [11] and related AI management and risk standards. Data protection authority / responsible ministry Clarify lawful data handling as the Data Protection Act moves through commencement and implementation, especially biometric and worker data. Operators and contractors Maintain AI inventories, tier systems by consequence, preserve logs, validate high- consequence uses and report material incidents. Universities and technical institutes Build local capability in data science, assurance, cybersecurity, mining engineering and environmental analytics.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 12 6. A 12-month implementation path Period Action 0-90 days Create a joint extractive AI working group. Issue a two-page interim advisory. Ask large operators to submit confidential inventories of Tier 2 and Tier 3 AI uses. Identify worker and environmental data categories needing special treatment. 3-6 months Publish a draft Guyana Extractive AI Assurance Protocol. Pilot the four-tier classification at two large operations and a selected regulatory workflow. Train inspectors and HSE personnel on AI evidence and failure modes. 6-9 months Introduce a standard AI assurance annex for relevant environmental and mining submissions. Establish a material AI incident reporting channel and a small regulator testing capability. 9-12 months Evaluate pilot evidence. Publish final guidance. Define where independent third-party assurance is required. Start an annual anonymised sector report on AI use, benefits, incidents and lessons. What success looks like Success is not a count of AI systems deployed. Success is a sector in which useful systems scale, high-consequence systems face stronger evidence requirements, failures are detected early, workers know when AI materially affects them, regulators can reconstruct important decisions, and executives retain clear accountability.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 13 7. Policy positions for debate No black-box excuse for legal duty. A company or agency should not defend a material failure by saying that the model produced the answer. Legal and managerial accountability stays with the responsible institution and person. Human review must be meaningful. Human approval is not a safeguard when the reviewer lacks time, information, competence or authority to reject the output. Local suppliers should not be excluded by opaque scoring. AI-assisted procurement should preserve a review path for vendors, especially where local-content objectives or SME participation are affected. Worker data deserves stricter treatment. Biometrics, fatigue indicators, location data and behavioural scores should face purpose limitation, access control, retention limits and a clear employment-policy basis. Environmental AI should produce evidence, not replace evidence. Remote sensing, anomaly detection and predictive systems should strengthen inspections and monitoring. They should not erase the need for calibrated instruments, field verification and accountable professional judgement. Regulators need their own technical capacity. A regulator that depends entirely on operator- supplied models cannot independently test claims, assumptions or system limitations.

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 14 8. Factual scrutiny audit The following audit records the most material factual checks performed before publication. It is included to separate verified evidence from projections, attributed claims and author proposals. Mining and quarrying estimated growth of 21% in 2025; gold declarations 484,321 oz Government estimate Verified against the 2026 Budget Speech, paragraphs 3.10-3.12. AskGov, MyGuyana Portal and e-ID are 2026 digital initiatives Government programme Verified against Budget 2026 and February 2026 public- service briefing. No claim made that all were fully operational by the evidence cut-off. Guyana-Cerebras project is up to 100 MW Announced MOU Verified against Government and Cerebras releases dated 12 November 2025. Described as an MOU/announced project, not an operating data centre. Data Protection Act 18 of 2023 [6][7] was enacted Verified law Verified against Parliament and Official Gazette. Section 1 makes commencement dependent on ministerial order. No commencement order was identified in the public sources reviewed. Mining licence process requires EPA environmental permit Verified administrative requirement Verified against GGMC published mining licence process. BHP reports 3bn litres water and 118 GWh energy savings from AI plant control Attributed company claim Verified against BHP release dated 27 May 2025. Kept as a BHP-reported outcome. OECD AI Principles [12] updated in 2024 Verified international policy source Verified against OECD. Principles include human oversight, transpare

AI ASSURANCE FOR GUYANA'S EXTRACTIVE SECTOR Ragunauth Ramsaroop | September 2026 | 15 robustness and accountability. ISO/IEC 42001 [11] published December 2023 Verified international standard Verified against ISO. Described as an AI management-system standard, not as a Guyanese legal requirement. NIST AI RMF functions are Govern, Map, Measure, Manage Verified framework Verified against NIST AI RMF resources. Described as voluntary guidance. ILO says digitalisation can improve OSH while introducing new risks Verified international research Verified against ILO 2025 global report. Used as a balanced policy finding. Four-tier risk model and six- pillar framework Author proposition Original analytical framework. Not represented as existing Guyanese law or policy.

papers.title: Nature as National Wealth: Financing Guyana's Biodiversity through Sovereign Leadership, Indigenous Stewardship and Disciplined Global Investment

pages.text: GUYANA / NATURE FINANCE 2026 INDEPENDENT EXECUTIVE WHITE PAPER Nature as National Wealth Financing Guyana's biodiversity through sovereign leadership, Indigenous stewardship and disciplined global investment. RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP Georgetown, Guyana | October 2026

THE AUTHOR'S POSITION The investment case for living natural capital Guyana has proven the financial relevance of keeping forests standing. The next challenge is more demanding: finance biodiversity itself without overstating ecological equivalence or treating speculative transactions as secured capital. This paper argues for a coordinated national nature-finance platform, three financing windows, a selective approach to five financial instruments and enforceable scientific, fiscal and community safeguards. Report at a glance Purpose. Set a credible policy and investment architecture. Approach. Evidence, instrument selection, project preparation and governance. Decision horizon. A 36-month stage-gated programme, subject to approval. Core rule. Verified results must precede claims of environmental value. Publication basis Prepared as independent analysis and a proposal for policy consideration. This report does not imply endorsement by the Government of Guyana, the Global Biodiversity Alliance or any financing institution. All conceptual investment values are illustrative. Cover photograph: Kanuku Mountains, Guyana. Pete Oxford. Reference photograph supplied by the commissioning reader. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH 02

READING GUIDE Contents A decision-oriented research paper in six parts. 01 The mandate Global financing gap, Guyana's record and the economic argument. 02 The instruments Five financing mechanisms and international precedents. 03 The architecture National platform, financing design and investment discipline. 04 The safeguards Rights, additionality, measurement and accountability. 05 From proposal to execution Pilot portfolio, measurable scorecard, financial diligence and 36-month roadmap. 06 Closing framework The Georgetown Compact, concluding judgment and evidence base. Evidence standard Verified historical evidence is distinguished from recommendations, transaction analogues and hypothetical financing assumptions. Numbered citations correspond to the linked reference register. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH 03

01 / EXECUTIVE BRIEF An investment thesis, not a conservation slogan The immediate opportunity is to convert biodiversity policy into financed, independently measured programmes without surrendering ecological or fiscal integrity. Core thesis. International beneficiaries of nature protection should participate in financing verifiable conservation outcomes. For Guyana, the appropriate response is not to monetise its entire biodiversity estate. It is to finance a prepared portfolio of projects with sound rights arrangements, disclosed costs and outcomes subject to independent review. The decision in front of policymakers Commission a feasibility assessment for a Guyana Nature Finance Platform aligned with LCDS 2030, existing budget processes and national biodiversity priorities. Structure three investment windows: community stewardship, ecosystem protection and nature-linked enterprise. Select financial tools according to project economics. Use an initial 12- to 18-month pilot programme to prove baseline quality, consent, legal readiness, buyer demand and monitoring costs before scale. Publish a public register differentiating proposals, legal commitments, disbursements and verified ecological outcomes. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 04

The measure of success is not the value assigned to nature. It is the amount of verified protection and lasting public benefit financed. CENTRAL RECOMMENDATION A comprehensive national facility should emerge from existing institutions through proper legal and financial review. This paper proposes an architecture for consideration, not an already established programme. 02 / GLOBAL FINANCE CONTEXT The funding system remains misaligned UNEP's State of Finance for Nature 2026 records the scale of global flows, using 2023 underlying data. [1] GLOBAL FINANCIAL FLOWS · 2023 UNDERLYING DATA US$7.3T Nature-negative financial flows US$220B Nature-based solutions More than 30 : 1 Harmful versus nature-positive flows NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 05

US$571 billion annually by 2030. UNEP estimates this level of nature-based investment is needed to support international biodiversity, climate and restoration objectives. The estimate is wider than biodiversity-specific finance and must not be equated with the Kunming-Montreal target. [1] US$200 billion annually by 2030. Global Biodiversity Framework Target 19 calls for mobilisation from all sources, including US$30 billion through international finance. These figures constitute global policy commitments, not financing presently available to Guyana. [2] Why the market fails Costs of protection fall largely on domestic institutions and communities, while ecological benefits extend across jurisdictions. Long investment horizons, weak ecological data, fragmented project pipelines and uncertain payers reduce the investability of conservation. 03 / GUYANA BASELINE A functioning national foundation Guyana's policy history already contains results-based finance, forest monitoring and community-oriented allocation arrangements. [3-5] 18M ha Approximate forest estate 85% Share of Guyana under forest US$353.5M Reported credit payments through March 2026 15% Carbon revenue allocated to village programmes NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 06

A credible timeline of policy and payment 2009 Low Carbon Development Strategy introduces a national low-carbon development model. 2009-2015 Norway performance-based cooperation: approximately US$230 million reported. [3] 2022 Hess carbon-credit purchase agreement: 37.5 million credits, minimum US$750 million in contracted future value. [4] 2026 Official LCDS portal reports US$353.5 million in cumulative credit payments to March. [3] Accounting discipline: A signed multi-year purchase agreement is not the same as cash received. Contract value, receipts, transfers and expenditure require separate reporting. 04 / THE STRATEGIC BOUNDARY Carbon is not biodiversity Forest-carbon experience provides institutions, but biodiversity requires different scientific measurements and different financial claims. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 07

Forest carbon Standardised tonnes of CO₂ equivalent support quantification and trading under specific rules. Baselines, leakage, permanence and registry accounting remain material. Biodiversity Ecological outcomes depend on location, habitat, species, condition and interdependent systems. A gain in one habitat rarely compensates for loss elsewhere. Three accounts must never be conflated 01 Ecological account What ecosystems exist? How are habitats and populations changing? Which conservation outcomes receive verification? 02 Economic-service account Which identifiable services flow from ecosystems, subject to which valuation assumptions and boundaries? 03 Financial account Which cash payments were committed or received, by whom, and under which rights, obligations and performance terms? A theoretical valuation of nature is not a public receivable, an investable cash flow or a sovereign financial asset. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 08

05 / THE POLICY CATALYST The proposition behind the headline An October 2026 Starting Point interview with former Colombian President Ivan Duque placed Guyana's biodiversity at the centre of a national-wealth debate. Duque's central observation, as represented in the source materials supplied for this paper, is that Guyana's GREEN SNAKE / PETE OXFORD · Images provided as reference materials Former Colombian President Iván Duque's observation, represented in the supplied Starting Point interview materials, is that Guyana's living natural assets deserve long-term financial recognition alongside its extractive wealth. He identified five financing mechanisms and emphasised a leading role for Indigenous communities. Finance demands more precision than equating ecological value with cash income. Every transaction needs an identifiable payer, a legitimate legal arrangement and an independently evidenced conservation outcome. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 09

Four strategic conclusions 01 Nature is productive capital Ecosystems support resilience, water and food security. An estimated economic value is not automatically a traded asset. 02 Compensation needs institutions Credible projects require enforceable agreements, dependable payers and accepted ecological verification methods. 03 Indigenous leadership changes design Rights, knowledge, benefit sharing and decision- making must shape the project from its initial stages. 04 Market development demands restraint Guarantees, bondholders and credit buyers face different risks. Claims of interchangeable biodiversity offsets demand special scrutiny. Analytical position: The interview motivates these independent recommendations. No proposed facility, market or financial commitment is presented as already authorised. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 10

06 / INSTRUMENT SELECTION Five tools. Five different financing logics. Instrument choice should follow the problem, the payer and the project's financial characteristics, rather than its environmental label. 01 Debt-for-nature conversion Sovereign refinancing savings Use only where the debt profile generates genuine net savings after transaction costs. 02 Credit guarantees Risk reduction for lenders Use where project cash flow exists but defined risks restrict affordable finance. 03 Biodiversity bonds Debt capital for eligible use Use with a creditworthy issuer, transparent repayment and an eligible project pipeline. 04 Biodiversity credits Payment for evidenced ecological outcomes Use with a valid baseline, buyer demand, rights, registry and defensible buyer claims. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 11

05 Outcome bonds Returns linked to agreed results Use with a reliable outcome payer, independent verification and contractual triggers. Recommendation: Start with simpler stewardship grants, performance-based contracts and project-preparation finance. Adopt bonds, guarantees or credits only when the underlying conditions support them. 07 / INSTRUMENT ONE Debt-for-nature conversion A sovereign liability-management transaction, not free conservation money. Debt-for-nature conversions refinance, exchange or repurchase eligible public debt and direct agreed financial benefits to conservation. A transaction succeeds only if net fiscal benefits survive all legal, financing, guarantee, Precedents with practical lessons BELIZE / 2021 Belize completed a major marine conservation debt conversion supported by a new financing structure. Its relevance is transaction design, long-term conservation commitments and independent management, not automatic transferability to Guyana. [10] ECUADOR / 2023 Ecuador's Galapagos conversion involved large-scale debt repurchases and a dedicated marine conservation commitment. Official reporting anticipated over US$450 million for conservation over time. Actual outcomes depend on implementation. [11] NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 12

The Guyana decision rule Require a published net-present-value analysis of pre- and post-transaction public debt service. Quantify contingent liabilities, guarantee fees, advisory charges and conservation spending commitments. Secure budgetary and legal oversight, with no restrictions inconsistent with national sovereignty. Reject a debt conversion where refinancing economics are unattractive. Assessment: Conditional relevance. The economics of Guyana's specific debt portfolio, rather than the popularity of the mechanism, must determine suitability. 08 / INSTRUMENT TWO Guarantees are risk tools, not revenue models Guarantees improve financing terms only when projects have viable repayment pathways and risks suited to contractual coverage. A development-bank or specialist guarantee offers protection against specified payment or credit risks. It does not establish an offtake market, create project revenue or demonstrate ecological impact. Financial reporting must distinguish the face amount of a guarantee from actual investment. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 13

Where a guarantee makes sense Investable revenue Nature tourism, environmental services or sustainable enterprise supported by defensible customer demand and a cash-flow forecast. Specific financing constraint Defined tenor, counterparty or credit barriers, rather than continuing operational losses. Transparent public exposure Document limits, pricing, recovery rights, contingent liabilities and fiscal disclosure arrangements. Screening sequence 01 Evidence of demand Identify customers, contracts and realistic demand. 02 Viable operations Review profitability, cash conversion and downside liquidity. 03 Identified risk Define the specific exposure requiring protection. 04 Guarantee pricing Compare guarantee cost with financing benefits. 05 Fiscal disclosure Record potential public liabilities and recourse. Assessment: Selective relevance for commercially grounded projects. Project preparation and market testing should precede guarantee negotiations. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 14

09 / INSTRUMENT THREE Bonds need repayment, not a green label A biodiversity-themed bond still represents a debt obligation. Environmental designation does not independently improve creditworthiness. A use-of-proceeds bond raises money against an issuer's repayment capacity and allocates proceeds to defined A use-of-proceeds bond raises money against an issuer’s repayment capacity, allocating proceeds to specified eligible expenditures. A credible bond framework identifies permitted projects, prohibited uses, selection criteria, proceeds management and public reporting. Six pre-issuance controls 01 Debt-service strength A creditworthy issuer and a credible plan to repay principal and interest. 02 Eligible pipeline Sufficient projects with defensible eligibility and implementation readiness. 03 Independent review External assessment of the financing framework before issuance. 04 Traceable proceeds Ring-fenced or otherwise traceable investment, spending and financial controls. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 15

05 Sound ecological indicators Methodologies proportionate to the environmental claims being made. 06 Annual accountability Transparent allocations and verified performance reporting. Instrument hierarchy For early biodiversity projects, grants or concessional facilities often fit better than sovereign borrowing. Bond issuance should follow a credible project pipeline and demonstrate value relative to conventional public financing. Assessment: Medium-term option. No issue should proceed without debt- sustainability assessment, investor testing and a verified eligible project pipeline. 10 / INSTRUMENT FOUR Biodiversity credits require the highest integrity threshold A credit should represent a robustly defined and evidenced ecological contribution. It should not become a universal licence to destroy habitat elsewhere. [7] Biodiversity has no single globally interchangeable measurement unit. A credit calculated from hectares alone risks ignoring habitat condition, species characteristics, local threats and ecological context. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 16

Seven questions for every project and buyer 01 Baseline What ecological condition existed before the intervention? 02 Additionality What measurable benefit results from the financed project? 03 Location Which precise habitat and ecological unit are covered? 04 Rights Whose land, knowledge and resource interests are affected? 05 Durability For how long should outcomes persist, and who bears reversal risk? 06 Claims What environmental statement is the buyer entitled to make? 07 Assurance Who independently verifies methodology, results and distribution of funds? Recommended market position: Prioritise credible contributions to protection and restoration. Do not assume biodiversity improvements in one ecosystem offset unrelated damage elsewhere. Every claimed unit requires defensible rights and registry arrangements. [7] NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 17

11 / INSTRUMENT FIVE Pay for verified conservation outcomes Outcome-linked structures connect finance to agreed performance, but somebody must contractually fund the payment. The 2024 World Bank Amazon Reforestation-Linked Bond provides an instructive example: US$225 million in bond principal supported a structure mobilising approximately US$36 million for reforestation, with a variable The World Bank’s 2024 Amazon Reforestation-Linked Bond provides a useful precedent. The US$225 million issue supported a mechanism mobilising approximately US$36 million for reforestation, with variable returns linked to carbon-removal performance. Bond principal and funds supporting conservation are different financial quantities. [8] How an outcome transaction works INVESTOR Commits capital → PROJECTDelivers activities → VERIFIERChecks results → PAYERFunds outcomes Potential applications in Guyana Watershed recovery Payment linked to verified water quality, riparian indicators and relevant ecological recovery. Habitat restoration A contract tied to independently verified changes in ecological condition. Community stewardship Agreed outcome or stewardship payments supported by a contracted financing source. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 18

Essential distinction: The issuer, conservation project, outcome payer and investor each hold distinct obligations. Adequate bridge financing is required if ecological verification occurs later than expected. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 19

12 / PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE One platform, three financing windows A nationally governed investment pipeline should prepare projects once, then match each project to an appropriate source of capital. The proposed Guyana Nature Finance Platform is a feasibility concept. Any establishment would require legal analysis, government decisions, consultation and agreement on oversight. The platform should complement existing LCDS RUPUNUNI SAV ANNAHS / PETE OXFORD · Images provided as reference materials The Guyana Nature Finance Platform is a feasibility proposal, not an established public institution. Any authorisation would require legal review, consultation, government decisions and clear oversight arrangements. Existing LCDS structures should not be duplicated or appropriated. Three separately financed investment windows 01 / Community stewardship Community-led ecosystem monitoring, governance, sustainable livelihoods and agreed conservation. Funding: grants and stewardship payments. 02 / Protection and restoration Priority habitats, watershed recovery, connectivity and rehabilitation beyond legal obligations. Funding: grants and outcome contracts. NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 20

03 / Nature-linked enterprise Viable tourism, environmental services or sustainable enterprise with identifiable revenues. Funding: equity, debt and selective guarantees. One coordinated project-preparation pipeline. Different instruments for different financial and ecological needs. Common controls across all windows: a public project register, rights due diligence, procurement standards, environmental monitoring, financial reporting and independent assurance. 13 / ILLUSTRATIVE CAPITAL MODEL Structure finance around risk and cash flow The following US$100 million capital illustration is a design scenario, not a fundraising target, financing commitment or forecast. A diversified facility requires different pools of capital. Grants finance public-good activities. Concessional NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 21

ILLUSTRATIVE CAPITAL STACK · US$100 MILLION · NOT COMMITTED $15M Grants and preparation $25M Concessional capital $60M Commercial capital The capital waterfall Grants first. Finance ecological baselines, rights-related engagement, project design, independent monitoring and public-good activities. Concessional resources second. Address justified financing gaps, not projects lacking any sustainable economic rationale. Commercial resources last. Require bankable contracts, customer demand, financing protections and clear repayment sources. A leverage ratio should report actual third-party financing mobilised, without double-counting guarantees, transfers within the facility or refinancing of existing obligations. 15% 25% 60% NATURE AS NATIONAL WEALTH RESEARCH EDITION · OCTOBER 2026 RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT POLICY WHITE PAPER 22

14 / STRESS-TEST DISCIPLINE Build a portfolio robust to zero credit sales A credible facility must preserve its conservation objectives when emerging markets do not produce revenue. Commercial biodiversity- credit demand remains uncertain. Investment models should therefore be tested against conditions that eliminate speculative credit income and delay performance-based disbursements. Biodiversity-credit demand remains uncertain. Conservation commitments must survive zero credit sales, delayed outcome payments and higher-than-expected monitoring costs. Downside scenarios and management responses Base case / verified funding Legally funded grants and contracts meet obligations. Response: release expenditure only against approved cash and milestones. Credit failure / zero sales Potential buyers do not sign contracts. Response: preserve core stewardship obligations without recognising uncommitted revenue. The near-term objective is to convert historical evidence into current technical, environmental, social and regulatory proof. 20.6 Mlb historical U3O8 estimate 129,000 m historical drilling 92.3 km2 licence area 10+ mineralised targets WHAT IS KNOWN Guyana has a credible path toward becoming an emerging uranium jurisdiction, but the case is not yet a mine-development case. The present opportunity is best described as an advanced exploration and national positioning opportunity. Kurupung already carries decades of geological work, a large historical drill database, a historical resource estimate of 20.6 million pounds U3O8, and more than ten additional mineralised targets. Global uranium demand is also strengthening as nuclear capacity expands and governments seek more secure fuel supply chains. Those two factors create strategic timing. They do not remove project risk. TECHNICAL GATE The most important technical issue is metallurgy. Historical hard-rock tests cited in the 2025 technical report achieved uranium extraction of up to 83%, alongside acid consumption of about 290 kg per tonne. If later work confirms similarly high reagent demand, process economics, logistics and residue management would require close attention. If new mineral processing lowers acid demand materially, the project profile improves. This variable deserves equal emphasis with grade and resource growth.
