GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 03 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The opportunity is strategic because the starting evidence base is unusually advanced. The case strengthens only if current resource, modern metallurgy, baseline quality and regulatory readiness progress together. Guyana has a credible path toward becoming an emerging uranium jurisdiction, but the case is not yet a mine-development case. The present opportunity is best described as an advanced exploration and national positioning opportunity. Kurupung already carries decades of geological work, a large historical drill database, a historical resource estimate of 20.6 million pounds U3O8, and more than ten additional mineralised targets. Global uranium demand is also strengthening as nuclear capacity expands and governments seek more secure fuel supply chains. Those two factors create strategic timing. They do not remove project risk. The central national question is broader than whether one deposit reaches production. Guyana is assessing whether a known uranium system in the Guiana Shield is the first visible part of a larger mineral province, whether national institutions are ready for uranium-specific regulation, and whether local value capture would justify the social and environmental burden of development. A strong policy response would treat geology, metallurgy, environmental protection, radiation safety, community rights, export security and fiscal design as one integrated decision process. Kurupung's evidence base is stronger than a normal greenfield prospect. Cogema and U3O8 Corp. completed about 129,000 metres of drilling between 1979 and 2012. The current licence area covers about 92.3 square kilometres. The historical resource estimate totals 20.64 Mlb

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 04 A 3 Mlb per year production concept provides a useful scale marker. At uranium prices of US$60 to US$120 per pound, gross annual sales would span about US$180 million to US$360 million before recovery losses, operating cost, royalty, tax, transport and financing. Ten years of 3 Mlb annual product equals 30 Mlb delivered product. With realistic recovery losses, a mine plan would need substantially more than 30 Mlb of in-situ inventory. Under simple illustrative assumptions, the required inventory falls near 35 to 40 Mlb before reserve conversion and operating contingency. Resource growth therefore sits on the critical path. Guyana already has several foundations needed for responsible advancement. The Mining Act and GGMC licensing system support prospecting and mining approvals. EPA mining EIA guidelines provide an established environmental assessment route. The Radiation Safety and Security Act 2023 supplies a national radiation governance foundation. Guyana joined the IAEA in 2015 and has safeguards arrangements in force. The Amerindian Act sets specific obligations where mining affects titled Village lands, contiguous lands and waterways. Uranium still requires additional implementing depth across worker exposure, NORM residues, secure transport, emergency response, product accounting and long-term residue stewardship. The recommended national strategy is staged. First, prove the resource, metallurgy and environmental baseline. Second, build uranium-specific regulatory capacity before any mine construction decision. Third, develop a transparent national value framework covering local employment, procurement, royalties, taxation, infrastructure sharing, rehabilitation security and

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 05 FIFTEEN KEY FINDINGS The strongest thesis is disciplined option value. Each finding separates what the evidence supports today from what still needs to be proven. 1 Advanced starting point Kurupung has about 129,000 m of historical drilling, 88,000 m of stored U3O8 Corp. core, four deposits in a historical resource estimate, and ten or more additional mineralised targets. 2 Historical resource, not current resource The 20.6 Mlb U3O8 estimate is historical. U92 states a qualified person has not completed enough work to classify it as a current mineral resource. A current estimate is planned after new drilling. 3 District-scale geological logic Deposits and targets follow magnetic-low corridors within the Kurupung Batholith. The repeatable structural and alteration controls support systematic exploration rather than isolated anomaly chasing. 4 Resource growth is essential A 10-year, 3 Mlb/y concept requires 30 Mlb of product. After mining and metallurgical losses, the in-situ requirement rises materially above 30 Mlb. 5 Grade offers support, not proof The cited indicated grade of 0.072% U3O8 sits above selected low-grade Namibian open-pit comparators. Economics still depend on geometry, strip ratio, recovery, reagents, infrastructure and capital. 6 Metallurgy is a major gate Historical hard-rock leach tests reported extraction up to 83% with acid consumption near 290 kg/t. Reagent optimisation belongs among the highest-priority workstreams. 7 Global demand is supportive The WNA 2025 reference case lifts uranium requirements from about 68,920 tU in 2025 to just over 150,000 tU by 2040. The 2026 Red Book sees 2050 requirements near 84,800 to 143,900 tU. 8 Supply security adds strategic

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 06 FIFTEEN KEY FINDINGS | CONTINUED The strongest thesis is disciplined option value. Each finding separates what the evidence supports today from what still needs to be proven. 9 Guyana has a mining platform Active gold development in Cuyuni-Mazaruni brings contractors, skills, logistics experience and regulatory familiarity closer to Kurupung than in an isolated frontier jurisdiction. 10 Uranium adds new regulatory demands Mining regulation alone is insufficient. Radiation protection, NORM residues, product security, occupational monitoring and export controls require uranium-specific operating rules. 11 Environmental standards require front-loading The Guiana Shield combines high biodiversity, forest value and important watersheds. Baseline data and residue design should start well before feasibility completion. 12 Community rights are a project-critical issue The Amerindian Act creates notification, impact and consent-related obligations in relevant settings. Guyana would benefit from a single authoritative mineral data register with dates, classification systems and status labels. 14 Domestic nuclear power is a separate question A uranium mine does not require a Guyanese nuclear power programme. GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 10 01 SECTION The global uranium reset Nuclear fuel demand is rising while supply security has returned to national energy policy. Uranium has returned to strategic-energy policy after more than a decade of underinvestment. The latest market cycle differs from a simple commodity rebound. Nuclear electricity is receiving renewed support from governments seeking firm low-carbon generation, from utilities extending reactor lives, from newcomer states studying nuclear deployment, and from technology companies seeking large volumes of reliable electricity for data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure. The World Nuclear Association's 2025 fuel report estimates 2025 reactor uranium requirements near 68,920 tonnes uranium. Its 2040 reference case exceeds 150,000 tU, with an upper case above 204,000 tU. The OECD-NEA and IAEA 2026 Red Book reports 418 commercial reactors operating as of 1 January 2025 and projects 2050 uranium requirements around 84,800 to 143,900 tU per year. The range reflects uncertainty in build rates, life extensions, policy and technology, yet both endpoints sit above current requirements. Supply response matters as much as resource abundance. The 2026 Red Book reports more than 8.1 million tU in identified resources recoverable below US$260/kgU, yet it also stresses the need for sustained investment to convert resources into operating mines. Exploration and development expenditure exceeded US$1.78 billion during 2023 and 2024, up about 46% from the prior two-year period. No new uranium mine began production during the period despite project approvals and restarts elsewhere. The implication for Guyana is clear: geology has value only after financing, licensin

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 11 Figure 1. Global uranium requirement scenarios. WNA and OECD-NEA/IAEA figures use different scenario frameworks and are shown together for directional context. EXECUTIVE READOUT Nuclear fuel demand is rising while supply security has returned to national energy policy.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 12 02 SECTION Why Guyana matters Guyana combines an established mining platform, an underexplored shield and Atlantic access. Guyana combines three features relevant to uranium development: established extractive industries, an underexplored Precambrian shield, and rising global strategic interest in secure mineral supply. Gold and bauxite created a long mining history. Oil development has strengthened national exposure to large-scale project finance, international operators, logistics and environmental regulation. The country's official language is English and its legal system is rooted in English common law, factors which reduce some transaction friction for international investors. The Cuyuni-Mazaruni region already hosts operating and development-stage gold projects. U92's October 2026 presentation places Aurora, Toroparu, Oko West and Omai within roughly 34 to 189 kilometres of Kurupung. Distance alone does not create shared infrastructure, but nearby mine activity matters. Contractors, aviation, camp services, heavy equipment support, laboratories, workforce mobility and regulatory experience are more developed than they were during the prior uranium exploration cycle. Guyana's Low Carbon Development Strategy 2030 adds an important policy lens. The strategy supports mineral mapping, more precise exploration, lower-impact mining and stronger integration of natural-resource development with biodiversity and forest protection. A uranium strategy aligned with LCDS 2030 would focus on precise targeting, minimal land disturbance, strong water protection, progressive rehabilitation and measurable local benefits. The country should avoid framing uranium as a race to production. A stronge

Source: U92 Energy Corp., Investor Presentation, October 2026, page 5. EXECUTIVE READOUT Guyana combines an established mining platform, an underexplored shield and Atlantic access.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 15 03 SECTION Exploration history and the evidence base Kurupung starts with decades of drilling, stored core and a substantial legacy technical dataset. Uranium exploration in the Kurupung-Aricheng area spans more than four decades. Cogema, now part of Orano, explored the area between 1979 and 1984 following earlier regional uranium work. The 2025 technical report states Cogema drilled 41,334 metres in 291 holes across 14 Aricheng-area targets. U3O8 Corp. later completed about 88,388 metres in 440 diamond drill holes between 2007 and 2012. U92's current public material rounds the total historical drilling to about 129,000 metres. The 2011 Fukushima accident changed uranium market sentiment and access to capital. Work paused in 2012 despite multiple defined deposits and additional targets. This history matters because current development does not begin from zero. Existing core, logs, assays, geophysics and geological interpretation shorten several exploration steps, provided verification work supports modern reporting standards. The stored core inventory has strategic value. U92 states about 88,000 metres of U3O8 Corp. core remains on the property in good condition. Re-logging, density work, confirmatory assays, spectral work, geometallurgy and modern structural interpretation have lower cost than recreating the entire historical programme. The historical database also supports target ranking before new drilling. Data age remains a constraint. Modern resource reporting requires verification, quality assurance, survey control, database integrity and current economic assumptions. The project therefore sits in an unusual middle ground: more advanced than a new discovery, yet not ready for

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 16 04 SECTION Geological setting and deposit model Repeatable mineralised corridors support a district-scale exploration thesis rather than isolated occurrences. Kurupung sits within Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Guiana Shield. Academic work describes the approximately 2.1 billion-year-old Kurupung Batholith as a sanukitoid intrusive complex within the Transamazonian-aged Mazaruni granite-greenstone terrane. Uranium mineralisation is associated with structural zones, sodium metasomatism and albitisation. The 2010 Mineralium Deposita study on Aricheng South links mineralisation with late-magmatic alteration, brannerite, uraninite and hydrothermal zircon. The current exploration model uses a practical geophysical signature. Mineralised structures occur along zones of reduced magnetism, interpreted as demagnetised corridors related to alteration and shearing. Deposits and many drilled targets align with these magnetic lows. This relationship gives the project a repeatable exploration vector and supports extension drilling along strike and at depth. The 2025 technical report identifies two broad structural styles: mineralisation along shear-zone boundaries and mineralisation within domain interiors dominated by east-trending orientations. Both styles support a three-dimensional target model rather than a shallow blanket deposit concept. The report also notes albitite-hosted uranium systems elsewhere extend to significant depth. Local continuity still requires drilling. Geological analogues matter for process and exploration thinking. Aricheng shares albitite-type characteristics with deposits in Brazil, Australia, Ukraine, Canada and other regions. The Lagoa Real district in Brazil offers

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 17 Figure 3. Historical deposits, targets and licence geometry within the Kurupung Project. Source: U92 Energy Corp., Investor Presentation, October 2026, page 10. EXECUTIVE READOUT Repeatable mineralised corridors support a district-scale exploration thesis rather than isolated occurrences.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 18 05 SECTION The historical resource: what it says and what it does not say The 20.6 Mlb estimate is meaningful historical evidence, but it is not a current mine-planning resource. The October 2026 investor presentation reports a 20.64 Mlb U3O8 historical resource estimate at a 0.03% cut-off. The cited split is 10.59 Mlb indicated at 0.072% U3O8 and 10.05 Mlb inferred at 0.067% U3O8. Aricheng West contributes 7.28 Mlb, Aricheng South 5.74 Mlb, Aricheng C 4.21 Mlb and Aricheng North 3.41 Mlb. U92 explicitly states the estimate is historical and is not being treated as a current mineral resource. The company notes the historical models used inverse-distance-squared estimation and a uranium price assumption of US$55/lb, with a recommended cut-off of 0.05% U3O8 at the time. A current resource update is planned after new drilling, with a pit-constrained estimate targeted for Q3 2027. This distinction is essential for national analysis. A historical resource is evidence of mineral endowment and exploration maturity. It is not a reserve, mine plan or guarantee of economic extraction. A current resource estimate would still require later technical studies, metallurgical recovery, geotechnical work, hydrogeology, environmental baseline, mine design, capital estimates and market assumptions before development confidence rises. Older national and international sources show different uranium figures for Guyana. The Ministry of Natural Resources mineral map published in 2025 displays an 8.4 Mlb Aricheng-Kurupung resource at 0.09%. The OECD-NEA/IAEA 2024 Red Book reports Guyana resource tonnages under a different cost and recoverability framework. These figures are not directly comparable. The dive

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 19 Figure 4. Historical resource distribution across the four cited deposits. EXECUTIVE READOUT The 20.6 Mlb estimate is meaningful historical evidence, but it is not a current mine-planning resource.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 20 06 SECTION Exploration upside: from four deposits to a mineralised corridor system Ten or more drilled targets create a credible resource-growth pathway beyond the four historical deposits. The strongest growth case rests on already drilled targets rather than purely conceptual anomalies. U92 reports more than 15,000 metres across 82 holes in ten additional mineralised target areas outside the four deposits used in the historical estimate. Accori North C alone accounts for more than 5,200 metres of drilling. Several historical intersections reported on the company project page exceed 0.07% U3O8 across meaningful drilled widths. The target inventory supports three growth directions. First, infill drilling would test whether known target zones reach the density and continuity needed for resource estimation. Second, step-out drilling along magnetic-low corridors would test lateral extensions. Third, deeper holes would test down-plunge continuity below the average historical drilling depth, which U92 places near 130 metres from surface across the property. A district-scale hypothesis requires more than repeated mineralisation. The evidence threshold should include continuity, grade distribution, geometry, metallurgical similarity, mineable widths and practical pit or underground shapes. A large number of anomalies without conversion into resource-quality tonnes adds exploration interest but limited mine value. National mineral mapping offers a parallel opportunity outside the current licences. Guyana's LCDS update describes a programme for detailed mineral maps across several key districts, including Mazaruni. Adding uranium-sensitive radiometric, magnetic, structural and geochemical la

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 21 Figure 5. Historical drilling across ten additional mineralised targets reported in the October 2026 presentation. EXECUTIVE READOUT Ten or more drilled targets create a credible resource-growth pathway beyond the four historical deposits.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 22 07 SECTION Discovery efficiency and the value of geological learning Better geological targeting has materially reduced the reported discovery cost per pound. The company presentation reports falling historical discovery cost per pound as the exploration model matured: about US$0.82/lb at Aricheng North, US$0.53/lb at Aricheng West, US$0.51/lb at Aricheng South and US$0.32/lb at Aricheng C. Those figures describe historical drilling expenditure divided by pounds in the historical estimate. They do not forecast future finding cost. The direction of the trend still carries strategic meaning. Early programmes spent more capital learning the system. Later drilling benefited from improved understanding of geophysics, soil geochemistry, structure and ore-body orientation. In a data-rich project, the highest-return exploration dollars often come from integrating old data before increasing metres drilled. Guyana should draw a broader lesson for mineral policy. National geoscience data is infrastructure. Airborne geophysics, modern geological maps, geochemical coverage, digital drill databases and open metadata reduce exploration waste and reduce land disturbance. The LCDS mineral mapping programme therefore has both investment and environmental value. For Kurupung, the next test of exploration efficiency is conversion. New drilling should be assessed on pounds added to current resource categories, confidence improvement, metallurgical information and mine-design relevance, not metres drilled alone.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 23 Figure 6. Historical discovery cost metrics reported by U92. These are retrospective project metrics, not forward cost guidance. EXECUTIVE READOUT Better geological targeting has materially reduced the reported discovery cost per pound.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 24 08 SECTION Scale test: what a 3 Mlb per year concept implies A 3 Mlb/y concept needs materially more than 30 Mlb in-situ once mining and metallurgical losses are included. U92 states a near-term objective of growing the resource to support an initial ten-year mine life at more than 3 Mlb U3O8 per year. This target offers a useful planning reference even before a feasibility study. A 3 Mlb annual product rate is similar to several conventional uranium operations or development projects and would make Guyana a meaningful new supplier rather than a marginal producer. The arithmetic shows why resource growth is central. Ten years at 3 Mlb per year equals 30 Mlb of final product. Mining recovery, dilution, metallurgical recovery, ramp-up and operating losses mean the required in-situ inventory would exceed 30 Mlb. At 95% mining recovery and 83% metallurgical recovery, the simple requirement is near 38 Mlb before reserve conversion and contingency. At 90% metallurgical recovery, the figure remains near 35 Mlb. The historical 20.64 Mlb estimate therefore represents a foundation rather than a complete ten-year inventory for the stated production objective. A current resource above the historical figure, followed by adequate reserve conversion, would be needed. The resource-growth threshold should be published transparently as project studies advance. At an indicative head grade near 0.067% to 0.072% U3O8 and 85% recovery, 3 Mlb annual output points to roughly 2.2 to 2.4 million tonnes of ore processed per year. At 340 operating days, this equates to around 6,500 to 7,100 tonnes per day. The exact figure changes with grade, recovery, dilution and plant availability.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 25 Figure 7. Illustrative in-situ inventory required to deliver 30 Mlb of U3O8 product over ten years. EXECUTIVE READOUT A 3 Mlb/y concept needs materially more than 30 Mlb in-situ once mining and metallurgical losses are included.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 26 09 SECTION Grade, mineability and peer context Grade supports the opportunity, but geometry, recovery, strip ratio and infrastructure determine economics. The historical indicated grade of 0.072% U3O8 is higher than the grades cited for selected Namibian open-pit peers in the source presentation. Langer Heinrich is shown near 0.05% U3O8, Tumas near 0.03% and Etango-8 near 0.024%. This comparison helps show why lower-grade uranium mining remains viable in some settings. Grade alone does not determine operating cost. Cigar Lake in Canada combines extraordinary grade with technically demanding underground mining and specialised processing. Namibian open pits benefit from different geometry, climate, infrastructure and mineralogy. Kurupung's economic profile will depend on strip ratio, ore-body geometry, weathering, comminution, recovery, acid demand, residue management, power cost, road and river logistics, labour productivity and capital intensity. A pit-constrained resource update planned for 2027 is therefore an important step. Pit constraints introduce geometry and economic parameters into resource reporting rather than treating all mineralised blocks equally. Later studies should test staged pits, starter zones, saprolite versus hard-rock feed, stockpiling strategy and any underground transition only if depth extensions justify it. The correct national message is measured: Kurupung's grade is not a weakness in isolation, and it is not proof of low cost. It is one positive input among several unresolved technical variables.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 27 Figure 8. Grade comparison with selected Namibian open-pit projects from the October 2026 presentation. EXECUTIVE READOUT Grade supports the opportunity, but geometry, recovery, strip ratio and infrastructure determine economics.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 29 10 SECTION Metallurgy: the project-defining technical gate Recovery and acid consumption are the most important technical variables to resolve before process selection. Metallurgy deserves more attention than promotional project summaries usually give it. The 2025 technical report states hard-rock uranium occurs mainly in brannerite, with lesser uraninite and romanite. Brannerite is refractory. Historical acid-leach test work achieved extraction of up to 83%, accompanied by acid consumption of about 290 kg/t. Saprolite mineralisation contains secondary uranium minerals dominated by torbernite, with historical test work showing lower initial extraction and scope for optimisation. High acid consumption creates several linked risks. Reagent purchase and transport increase operating cost. On-site storage expands safety requirements. Neutralisation increases reagent and residue volumes. Residue chemistry affects tailings design and closure. Supply interruptions create production risk. Each issue is more pronounced in a remote hinterland setting. The old test result should not be treated as a final process design. Modern metallurgical work should test mineral sorting, radiometric sorting, pre-concentration, selective grinding, carbonate rejection, flotation options, pressure or atmospheric leach conditions, oxidants, temperature, residence time, acid recycle and residue neutralisation. Geometallurgical domains should separate saprolite, transition and fresh rock rather than apply one recovery assumption across the deposit. A simple scale check shows the importance. If a future 2.2 Mt/y plant consumed 290 kg/t of sulfuric acid, annual acid demand would exceed 600,000 tonnes. A materially l

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 30 11 SECTION Processing concept and throughput implications Process design must balance recovery, reagent intensity, water, residue volumes and operating reliability. A conventional hard-rock uranium flowsheet would likely involve crushing, grinding, leaching, solid-liquid separation, uranium recovery from solution, precipitation, drying and packaging of uranium ore concentrate. The final design depends on mineralogy and test work. No final flowsheet has been established publicly for a new Kurupung operation. Throughput near 2 to 2.5 Mt/y places the concept within a scale familiar to Guyana's mining sector. The unusual element is radiological and chemical control. Process water, dust, radon, residues, concentrate packaging and occupational exposure require uranium-specific design standards from the start. Energy supply also affects cost and emissions. A future mine should compare grid connection options, isolated thermal generation, solar plus storage, and hybrid systems. Guyana already has operating experience with renewable-energy investment at remote mining sites, which reduces technology novelty. A feasibility study should compare lifecycle cost, reliability and emissions rather than select an energy system from headline capacity alone. Water balance is equally important. A tropical wet environment changes the design problem from the arid settings of Namibia and Australia. Stormwater separation, contact-water storage, seepage control, diversion capacity and wet-season operating resilience should shape the plant and residue facility layout before final siting.

Uranium residues remain a long-term obligation after final product leaves the site. Tailings retain most of the original ore mass and contain decay products and other constituents. Design should therefore focus on physical stability, seepage control, water quality, radon pathways, erosion resistance, flood resilience and long-term monitoring. Guyana's high rainfall places water management at the centre of residue design. Probable maximum precipitation, catchment controls, diversion channels, freeboard, spillways, seepage collection and emergency water storage require conservative design. Climate-change scenarios should form part of closure design rather than a separate sustainability appendix. The IAEA's guidance for uranium production and naturally occurring radioactive material provides a strong reference for national rules. Guyana should align licensing conditions with international good practice while retaining site-specific requirements for tropical hydrology and forest environments. Financial assurance also matters. Closure bonds or equivalent security should cover progressive rehabilitation, final closure, long-term monitoring and corrective work. The mechanism should be transparent and updated as the mine plan changes.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 35 15 SECTION Radiation safety, safeguards and security Guyana has a legal foundation, but uranium production needs specialised monitoring, reporting and security systems. Guyana enacted the Radiation Safety and Security Act No. 10 of 2023, giving the country a stronger legal base before any uranium mine decision. Guyana has been an IAEA Member State since 2015 and has safeguards arrangements in force. These foundations reduce institutional distance, but uranium mining and milling would still require specialised regulations, inspectors, laboratories, monitoring systems and emergency protocols. Occupational controls should address gamma exposure, radon and radon progeny, airborne long-lived alpha activity, contaminated dust, process chemicals and concentrate handling. Personal dosimetry, area monitoring, medical surveillance, training and controlled-area procedures belong in mine design rather than post-construction operating manuals. Nuclear safeguards for uranium production differ from reactor safeguards. Mining and milling sit at the front of the fuel cycle, with state reporting and export-import obligations linked to material form and safeguards agreements. Guyana should work directly with the IAEA on reporting thresholds, material accounting interfaces and additional protocol implications where relevant. Physical protection focuses on concentrate storage, transport routes, access control, tamper resistance and incident response. Uranium ore is not a nuclear explosive material, yet concentrate remains a regulated strategic commodity. Clear public communication is important so security measures do not create unnecessary fear or secrecy.

Health-risk communication should compare projected doses with natural background and regulatory limits without minimising uncertainty. Benefit design should favour durable value. Training, apprenticeships, local procurement, road safety, health services, communications and enterprise development usually outlast one-time donations. GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 38 17 SECTION Legal and permitting framework Existing mining and EIA systems provide a base, but uranium-specific terms and agency coordination are required. Guyana's Mining Act 1989 and GGMC licensing system provide the core mineral-tenure pathway. GGMC guidance states prospecting licences generally run for three years with two one-year renewal rights, subject to work programmes, budgets, reporting and performance bonds. Mining licence applications require technical and economic studies, mine plans and environmental documentation, with EPA environmental permitting forming part of the approval sequence. The EPA's mining EIA guidelines provide a structured assessment process. Uranium development should sit within this framework, with uranium-specific terms of reference covering radiological baseline, residue management, occupational exposure, concentrate transport and long-term stewardship. A large-scale uranium mine would likely involve multiple agencies beyond GGMC and EPA. Radiation regulators, customs, security agencies, transport authorities, labour regulators, local government and Amerindian institutions would each hold defined roles. A single inter-agency project protocol would reduce duplicated requests and regulatory gaps. Fiscal terms should remain transparent and stable. Uranium projects are long-duration investments with large sunk costs and commodity-price exposure. Government should preserve the right to capture fair value while avoiding bespoke uncertainty which raises financing cost. Clear royalty, tax, import, depreciation and rehabilitation-security rules improve both public revenue planning and investor discipline.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 39 18 SECTION Institutional readiness: what Guyana should build before construction A small, competent multi-agency capability should be built before any construction decision. Uranium production requires a capability stack broader than conventional mining. The priority is not a large new bureaucracy. The priority is a small, competent system with clear authority, specialist training, reliable laboratories, inspection procedures and access to international expertise. A national Uranium Development Working Group should bring together the Ministry of Natural Resources, GGMC, EPA, the radiation safety authority, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, labour regulators, customs, security and transport agencies. Its first task should be a regulatory gap assessment against IAEA guidance and experience from established uranium jurisdictions. Laboratory capacity needs early planning. Baseline and compliance programmes require low-level radiological analysis, uranium-series radionuclides, water chemistry and quality assurance. Guyana should decide which analyses belong in domestic accredited laboratories and which should use international reference laboratories during early stages. Emergency readiness should cover chemical spills, concentrate incidents, worker contamination events, transport accidents and extreme weather. Multi-agency exercises before commissioning would test responsibility and communications.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 40 19 SECTION Economics: the opportunity range The opportunity is commercially material, but no public feasibility study yet establishes project economics. No public feasibility study establishes Kurupung economics. Any valuation in this paper is therefore illustrative. A 3 Mlb/y product rate gives a gross-sales range of US$180 million at US$60/lb, US$240 million at US$80/lb, US$300 million at US$100/lb and US$360 million at US$120/lb. Gross sales are not profit, cash flow or national revenue. The largest economic unknowns are resource scale, strip ratio, metallurgical recovery, reagent consumption, capital intensity, power, logistics and uranium contract pricing. Uranium mines often sell under a mix of long-term contracts and market-related mechanisms rather than a single daily spot price. Financing also depends on customer quality, contract tenor and jurisdictional risk. Project economics should be stress-tested under lower prices, delayed ramp-up, lower recovery, higher acid consumption, wet-season disruptions and higher closure cost. A mine which works only at the top of a price cycle offers weaker national value than a mine with resilience across several market conditions. Government revenue modelling should separate royalty, corporate tax, payroll taxes, import duties, withholding taxes and state fees. Local procurement and wages should be reported separately from fiscal receipts to avoid double counting national benefit.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 42 20 SECTION National value creation and local content The strongest national value lies in capability transfer, technical employment, local procurement and durable infrastructure. The national prize is broader than export revenue. A successful uranium project would create demand for geology, drilling, environmental science, radiation protection, engineering, construction, camp services, transport, laboratories, security, maintenance and professional services. Guyana already has parts of this supply chain through gold, bauxite and oil. Local-content strategy should focus on capability transfer rather than headline percentages. High-value technical roles require education pathways several years before commissioning. Scholarships, apprenticeships, university partnerships and vendor training should target radiation protection, mineral processing, laboratory science, tailings management, instrumentation and heavy maintenance. Procurement rules should distinguish goods Guyana is able to supply competitively from specialised imports needed for safety or performance. Forcing local sourcing where capability is not ready raises cost and project risk. A supplier-development programme with quality, safety and financing support produces stronger long-term results. Infrastructure co-benefits should be negotiated carefully. Roads, communications and power upgrades offer public value where design, access, maintenance and security permit shared use. Project infrastructure should not be counted as a national benefit if access remains exclusive or public maintenance costs rise after closure.

GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 43 21 SECTION Strategic positioning in the Americas Guyana is best positioned as a responsible upstream uranium supplier, not as a full fuel-cycle jurisdiction. Guyana's geography gives it access to Atlantic trade routes and places a potential uranium source within the Western Hemisphere. Security of supply now matters to utilities and governments alongside price. A stable Guyanese source would add geographic diversity to a market concentrated in Kazakhstan, Canada, Namibia, Australia and a small group of other producers. Guyana should position itself as a responsible upstream supplier rather than attempt to replicate the full nuclear fuel cycle. Mining and uranium concentrate production are one segment. Conversion, enrichment and fuel fabrication require different technologies, capital, security systems and non-proliferation controls. Vertical expansion should occur only where a separate national case exists. Offtake strategy should prioritise credible counterparties, transparent pricing mechanisms and alignment with non-proliferation obligations. Long-term contracts often improve project financing because they reduce revenue uncertainty. Government interest is best protected through transparent fiscal terms and compliance, not direct interference in normal commercial contracting unless national security requires it. The strongest national brand would be low-impact, high-governance uranium from a country already known for forest-climate stewardship. This claim requires proof through monitoring, rehabilitation, community outcomes and transparent reporting.

Government completes a uranium regulatory gap assessment and creates an inter-agency working group. Phase 2, 2027 to 2029: project definition. Apply staged construction controls, independent tailings review, radiation-protection systems, community monitoring and transparent performance reporting. The schedule is illustrative. Resource results, permitting and economics will determine actual timing. Parallel national track, 2026 to 2035: expand mineral mapping for uranium and related critical-mineral signatures, modernise the national mineral data register, build university programmes, strengthen radiological laboratories and join international peer networks for uranium production safety.

Global uranium demand and supply-security policy add favourable timing. The opportunity is not yet proven because the current development case still depends on resource conversion, scale, metallurgy, mine design, environmental performance, social acceptance, regulation and financing. The single most important discipline is to keep these uncertainties visible. Historical pounds should not be treated as reserves. Grade should not be treated as cost. Global demand should not be treated as project economics. Guyana's best strategy is evidence-led and staged. International support from the IAEA and experienced uranium jurisdictions would shorten the institutional learning curve. If the technical case strengthens, Guyana has a path toward becoming a new uranium supplier in the Americas during a period of structural nuclear growth. GUYANA'S URANIUM OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC WHITE PAPER Ragunauth Ramsaroop | October 2026 73 Guyana uranium: one-page strategy A staged national framework keeps optionality while protecting technical, environmental and institutional discipline. Question Answer Does Guyana have credible uranium potential? Yes. Kurupung provides a well-drilled, known uranium system with a 20.6 Mlb historical estimate and substantial target inventory. Is a mine proven? No. Current resource conversion, metallurgy, mine design, environmental performance, social outcomes and economics remain unresolved. What is the strongest near-term value driver? A current resource estimate combined with modern metallurgical results, especially lower reagent intensity. What is the biggest technical risk? Hard-rock metallurgy and acid demand, followed by resource scale and water-tailings design. What is the biggest national governance task? Build uranium-specific regulatory capacity across radiation safety, NORM residues, transport, security and long-term stewardship. What should Guyana avoid? Rushing to production, conflating uranium mining with domestic nuclear power, or treating historical pounds as mineable reserves. What should success look like by 2028? Current resource, modern metallurgy, multi-season baseline, defined regulatory pathway, credible community process and scoping-level economics. What should success look like by 2035? Either a responsibly operating uranium mine with strong national value or a well-supported decision not to mine. Both outcomes reflect disciplined governance. FOCUS AREA Core position Guyana should treat uranium as a strategic national option. The value of the option rises as evidence quality, regulatory capability and environmental credibility improve.

pages.text: RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 1 Standing Forests, Measurable Outcomes The Climate Value of Forest Protection, Governance and Carbon Accountability Ragunauth Ramsaroop 26 September 2026 Abstract An independent evidence synthesis and audit-ready evaluation protocol for protected forests, causal climate benefits, Guyana reference-level accounting, rights and forest finance. Expanded second edition. Original cover illustration: layers of forest canopy representing the relationship between existing forest carbon and monitored landscape change. INDEPENDENT RESEARCH | FOREST CARBON | CONSERVATION GOVERNANCE

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 2 Publication statement Author: Ragunauth Ramsaroop Publication type: Independent research white paper; secondary evidence synthesis and methodological framework Release: Version 2.0, 26 September 2026 Location: Georgetown, Guyana Rights: © 2026 Ragunauth Ramsaroop. All rights reserved. Contact: ragunauthramsaroop.com This independent paper was prompted by Conservation International’s public explanation of a 2023 scientific study. All interpretations, original analytical frameworks, illustrative models and policy options presented here are independent. Conservation International, the study authors, the Guyana government and the institutions cited did not sponsor, commission, review or endorse this publication. No claim of original satellite-data reanalysis or independent peer review is made. The source-derived tables are subject to their stated transcription and accounting boundaries. This expanded second edition adds a primary-source crosswalk for Guyana’s UNFCCC 2025 assessment, an updated 320-study econometric meta-analysis, explicit audit tests, a new evidence matrix and a fully specified research design. It remains a secondary synthesis rather than a completed original spatial evaluation. Numerical results attributed to published studies retain their original dates, geographical coverage, assumptions and units. Readers should consult the underlying research and the cited primary data documentation when using results for regulatory submissions or financial transactions. Citation suggestion: Ramsaroop, R. RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 4 Executive summary Protecting a forest preserves a standing stock of carbon, but designation alone does not establish how much climate benefit occurred because the forest was protected. The difference matters for national planning, biodiversity strategies, conservation investment, corporate sustainability reporting and carbon-credit claims. A carbon inventory answers where carbon exists. A counterfactual analysis asks what likely would have happened in the absence of protection. A credible climate-finance claim needs still more evidence: suitable baselines, demonstrated additionality, quantified leakage, durability provisions, safeguards and independent verification. In 2023, Duncanson and colleagues used approximately 412 million observations from NASA’s Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) and statistical matching to examine the carbon effectiveness of protected areas. Within the satellite mission’s approximate 52 degrees north to 52 degrees south coverage, the researchers estimated 61.43 ± 0.31 billion tonnes of protected-area aboveground carbon and 9.65 ± 0.88 billion tonnes of additional carbon associated with protected status. Protected areas held, on average, 28% more aboveground carbon than their ecologically matched unprotected comparators. These are the study’s estimates, not new measurements generated for this white paper [1]. The distinction between total stock and attributed difference changes the interpretation. Approximately 84% of the estimated protected-area aboveground carbon stock in the study was not assigned to protection as an incremental effect. The 9.65-billion-tonne estimate represents a model- based comparison of standing aboveground carbon. An equivalent ca

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 5 The practical finding of this review is methodological. A credible assessment should report five separate accounts: the total carbon currently stored; observed annual forest loss; the counterfactual difference associated with protection; the risk-adjusted durability of any attributed benefit; and conservation outcomes beyond carbon. The updated Forest Protection Performance Ledger, introduced in this paper, holds these accounts separately. Such separation helps prevent overstatement, supports independent audit and enables comparison without treating a hectare designated on paper as equivalent to a hectare with demonstrated ecological outcomes. For Guyana, the distinction has immediate analytical value. National jurisdictional forest-carbon accounting under the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions and site-level performance monitoring address different questions. Guyana’s Protected Areas Commission identifies distinct management arrangements and ecosystems across Kaieteur, Kanuku Mountains, Shell Beach, Iwokrama and the Kanashen Amerindian Protected Area. An independent site-level assessment should integrate protected-area boundaries, national forest-monitoring records, community evidence, aboveground biomass measurements and pre-specified comparison areas. Such work should avoid adding site- level estimates to already-accounted national credits or assigning newly calculated carbon-credit revenue without a corresponding registry and accounting basis [9–12]. This second edition offers an independent synthesis, a detailed implementation framework, contrasting international case studies, transparent worked examples, a finance-integrity checklist and a reproducibility roadmap. It does not claim a n

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 6 Five principal findings One. Carbon stock and causal impact are different quantities. A forest might remain intact because of accessibility, terrain, land tenure, low economic pressure or local management rather than formal protection alone. Matching reduces observable differences but does not eliminate unmeasured confounding. Two. The climate contribution of protection varies substantially. The 2023 study reports strong aggregate aboveground-carbon differences, with tropical moist forests and Brazil contributing a major share. It also identifies protected areas with little observed additionality and others with lower carbon than matched unprotected areas [1]. Three. Forest degradation matters alongside clearing. Selective logging and structural losses reduce forest carbon even where an optical satellite continues to classify a pixel as forest. Lidar, repeated biomass products and well-designed field inventories provide complementary evidence. Four. Climate value has multiple risk dimensions. Displaced clearing, fire, drought, weak tenure, management gaps, insecure funding and carbon-accounting overlap all affect attribution and durability. These risks belong in results tables rather than in small-print disclaimers. Five. A credible monitoring system separates observation from interpretation. Remote-sensing measurements, a defensible counterfactual, verified governance information and an auditable data history perform different roles. None should substitute for the others. 1. Why standing forests require a different performance measure Figure 1. An original conceptual model of forest-protection mechanisms, confounding and climate risk. Dotted links represent potential competing explanations,

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 7 The central proposition of this paper is therefore narrower than a general endorsement of protected areas. Formal protection represents a potentially important institutional mechanism for retaining forest carbon, especially where credible conversion pressure exists. Its measured climate effect depends on what the protected landscape would otherwise have experienced, on the stability of management outcomes, and on the carbon pools included in the assessment. Evidence from a humid tropical reserve should not be transferred automatically to peatland, boreal forest, dry woodland or low-stature mangrove ecosystems. A useful illustration concerns two forests, each holding one million tonnes of aboveground carbon. The first faces immediate road expansion and agricultural conversion. The second lies in a remote location without documented commercial pressure. Their current stock is identical, but the additional climate impact of a new conservation intervention may differ substantially. The calculation changes again if the first intervention displaces clearing to the adjacent district, or if the second forest contains major cultural and biodiversity values unrelated to near-term emissions reduction. A sound decision record treats these attributes separately. This paper uses a three-layer evidence model. The first layer is descriptive inventory: land cover, legal boundaries, vegetation structure, carbon stocks and observed change. The second is quasi- causal evaluation: matched controls, pre-intervention trends and alternative counterfactuals. The third is implementation integrity: governance, safeguards, financing, leakage, reversals, public disclosure and conflict checks. The analytical standard rise

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 8 2. How protected forests affect climate 2.1 A stock, a flow and a counterfactual Carbon enters forests through photosynthesis and accumulates in living wood, roots, soils and other pools. Forest respiration, decomposition, fire, harvest and land conversion release carbon. A stock is the quantity present at a given time. A flow is the quantity entering or leaving during a stated period. A protected-area evaluation needs to record both, but should not replace one with the other. A single satellite snapshot of high carbon density cannot demonstrate annual net sequestration. The retained stock associated with protection is a difference between observed carbon at a measurement date and the estimated amount expected under a credible unprotected comparison. The term avoided emissions applies when the counterfactual difference is attributable to reductions in losses that otherwise would have transferred carbon to the atmosphere. Enhanced forest growth, delayed harvest, shifting emissions among pools and changing wood-product storage complicate the translation from a standing-carbon difference into atmospheric emissions. Time, geographic domain and the fate of disturbed biomass are therefore material components of the estimate. 2.2 Two routes to a positive carbon difference Protection might prevent complete stand replacement, such as clearing for agriculture. Alternatively, protection might limit partial degradation while maintaining the forest canopy. A third mechanism involves enhanced recovery after previous disturbance. These processes leave different remote-sensing signatures. A tree-cover-loss algorithm detects conspicuous canopy removal, whereas repeated lidar, radar or field biomass measuremen

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 9 statements should separate physical reversal from changes in legal designation, community consent, finance continuity and measurement uncertainty. The appropriate reporting horizon depends on the purpose: ecological management, national inventory, public expenditure evaluation or carbon-credit issuance. These purposes should not be compressed into a single undifferentiated carbon number. 3. What the global evidence demonstrates Figure 2. The published protected-area stock and matched, protection-associated increment in Duncanson et al. (2023), both in Gt C. The pale segment is arithmetic, not a separately measured forest class. 3.1 The 2023 GEDI study Duncanson and colleagues examined protected areas using approximately 412 million GEDI lidar observations, matched one-kilometre protected-area pixels with ecologically similar unprotected pixels and analysed canopy structure and aboveground carbon around 2020. The matching design incorporated climate, ecological category, country, land-cover characteristics and human-pressure variables representing conditions around 2000. A ten-kilometre exclusion zone around protected- area boundaries helped reduce mixed-pixel and immediate spillover complications. Pixels fully inside protection boundaries formed the principal treatment sample [1]. The study reported 61.43 ± 0.31 Gt C in protected-area aboveground woody vegetation across its observational domain. Its published estimate of additionally preserved carbon associated with protected status was 9.65 ± 0.88 Gt C. Protected sites averaged 28% higher aboveground carbon than matched comparators, and approximately 62.7% of analysed forested protected areas showed significantly higher carbon than their mat

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 10 3.2 Quantities that should not be conflated Published metric Reported value Interpretation Principal boundary Protected-area aboveground carbon stock 61.43 ± 0.31 Gt C Woody carbon located inside sampled protected areas GEDI observational domain [1] Additional carbon associated with protection 9.65 ± 0.88 Gt C Estimated difference from matched unprotected counterfactuals Dependent on matching and attribution assumptions [1] Mean matched aboveground-carbon difference 28% Average relative difference in the analysed comparison Not a universal site- specific rate [1] Forested protected areas with higher carbon 62.7% Share of studied forested protected areas with significant positive difference Site-level heterogeneity [1] Global forest area in FAO FRA 2025 4.14 billion ha Officially reported forest extent Different definitions and global population [2] Average annual deforestation, 2015– 2025 10.9 million ha Gross permanent forest conversion rate in FRA Not equivalent to annual Hansen tree- cover loss [2, 14] The reported uncertainty of ±0.31 Gt for total stock and ±0.88 Gt for associated additional stock reflects uncertainty as estimated by the source study. It should not be presented as exhaustive uncertainty across biomass-model bias, protected-area boundary errors, imperfect counterfactual comparability, baseline differences or political and ecological changes after observation. These additional uncertainties call for separate stress tests. 3.3 Implications for interpretation A large protected-area stock establishes the importance of existing carbon assets. The smaller attributed difference estimates the additional aboveground stock associated with protection under the published model. Neith

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 11 assumptions about policy, land-use pressure and enforcement [4]. Tropical forest studies using matched controls and quasi-experimental methods have estimated meaningful reductions in loss attributable to protection in various regions, while documenting weaker outcomes elsewhere [3, 5, 6]. The precise effect depends on site selection, a clear definition of treatment, forest pressure and the reference period. A 2013 systematic review of protected-area outcomes found evidence of reduced habitat loss in many settings but identified limitations in comparative evidence and major variation in management and monitoring [3]. Comparative research into human pressure and forest integrity likewise supports assessing real ecological performance rather than the administrative count of protected hectares [6, 8]. A global average obscures the distribution: large benefits in high-pressure forests can coexist with negligible short-term additionality in remote sites and negative effects in poorly governed locations. 3.5 Indigenous and community-governed forests Legal designation is not synonymous with effective stewardship, and government-managed conservation is not the only governance arrangement. A pan-tropical analysis of Indigenous Lands, protected areas and overlapping Indigenous-protected landscapes during roughly 2010–2018 found reduced deforestation in Indigenous Lands relative to matched non-protected comparators, along with broadly comparable reductions in degradation under several regional comparisons [7]. A separate study of tropical forest integrity identified strong outcomes in overlapping protected- Indigenous areas while also finding regional differences between land-governance categories [8].

RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH STANDING FORESTS • SEPTEMBER 2026 12 accounting and displacement. The first question may be answered with descriptive remote-sensing data; the second requires an identification strategy; the third additionally requires emissions factors, timing, permanence and a defined geographical accounting boundary. No single remote- sensing layer answers all three. Nolte and colleagues’ 2013 study examined 292 protected areas in the Brazilian Amazon, testing governance and location under differing levels of deforestation pressure. Their findings emphasize heterogeneity: all studied protection regimes reduced deforestation, but the relationship of strict protection, sustainable use and Indigenous lands to forest-loss pressure differed. The result is geographically and historically bounded, and it neither establishes a universal governance ordering nor eliminates potential unobserved confounding [32]. Related evidence from Acre illustrates why different allocation of protection regimes across high- and low-pressure land can alter an apparent comparison [33]. Why comparison design determines credibility 4.1 The protected-area placement problem Authorities often establish protected areas in places with unusual terrain, lower agricultural suitability, limited road access or lower pre-existing commercial demand. A simple average comparing carbon inside all protected sites with carbon outside would mix selection effects with protection effects. Remote high-altitude reserves may have remained forested even without a legal designation. Accessible lowland reserves may face much greater conversion pressure. The relevant question is what each protected site would have experienced under a credible alternative institutional arrangement. Statistical matching addresses observed placement differences by comparing sites with similar pre- treatment characteristics. Exact matches on country, biome and ecological region restrict comparisons to broadly similar contexts. Matching on baseline forest cover, elevation, slope, rainfall, distance to transport networks and earlier human pressure further improves comparability. Balance diagnostics should demonstrate the remaining differences rather than assume they are immaterial. 4.2 The unobserved-variable problem Matching does not prove that protected and unprotected locations were otherwise identical. Carbon calculations and communication controls B.1 Units and conversion One gigatonne of carbon is one billion metric tonnes of elemental carbon. A carbon-dioxide mass equivalent for complete oxidation uses the molecular-mass ratio 44/12. Under this purely physical conversion, 9.65 Gt C corresponds to approximately 35.38 Gt CO2 and ±0.88 Gt C corresponds to approximately ±3.23 Gt CO2. The total protected woody stock of 61.43 Gt C corresponds to approximately 225.24 Gt CO2 if all carbon were completely oxidised. These conversions do not indicate actual releases, annual emissions, additional removals or credits. Report the original carbon unit before presenting any converted equivalent. For a hypothetical 100,000-hectare landscape with modelled aboveground biomass density of 180 tonnes dry matter per hectare, a 0.49 carbon fraction produces an estimated 8.82 million tonnes of aboveground carbon. Other carbon pools remain excluded. The example is arithmetic, not a new observation at a real site. THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 2 CHAPTER 00 Publication Note and Scope A decision-grade synthesis for governments, boards, investors and resource-sector leaders. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ This paper examines the emerging resource-security system linking minerals, energy, electricity grids, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, trade corridors, industrial policy, finance and strategic alliances. The analytical horizon extends from 2026 to 2040, while quantitative evidence uses information available through 11 October 2026. The paper separates observed data from institutional forecasts and from author scenario analysis. Historical values are described as actual or estimated by the source. Forward values are identified as projections, outlooks or scenarios. Monetary figures are nominal US dollars unless a source states otherwise. Installed power capacity, electricity generation and energy investment are treated as separate measures. Source priority is given to primary public institutions and official policy instruments. Core evidence comes from the International Energy Agency, World Trade Organization, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, UN Trade and Development, International Renewable Energy Agency, US Geological Survey, NATO and official US-EU policy documents. Fast-moving conflict and market developments are date-stamped to the evidence cut-off. CORE THESIS The next phase of global economic competition will turn on the security, cost and speed of access to integrated resource systems. Geology matters. Processing, electricity, technology, infrastructure, capital and alliances determine who converts geology into strategic power. CHAPTER 00 Contents Executive map of the paper. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Section Purpose Executive Summ

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 3 CHAPTER 00 Executive Summary Resource security is becoming the operating system of industrial policy, energy policy, technology policy and national security. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ The world economy in 2026 is not deglobalizing in a simple or uniform direction. Trade remains large, digital and technology- linked trade is expanding rapidly, and cross-border capital still seeks scale. The structure of interdependence is changing. Governments and corporations are placing a higher premium on resilience, strategic control and trusted supply relationships. WTO evidence describes a multilateral system under its most sustained pressure in eight decades, while UNCTAD describes a selective reorganization of trade around geoeconomic priorities. (WTO, 2026a; UNCTAD, 2026b) Three forces now reinforce each other. First, the 2026 Middle East energy shock exposed persistent dependence on narrow maritime and energy corridors. Second, the AI investment cycle is translating digital ambition into physical demand for electricity, grids, semiconductors, cooling, storage and minerals. Third, critical-mineral concentration has shifted from a theoretical risk to an operating constraint as export controls, quotas and licensing measures spread. (IEA, 2026a; IEA, 2026b; UNCTAD, 2026a) The scale is large. IEA estimates global energy investment at US$3.4 trillion in 2026, with US$2.2 trillion directed to renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, low-emissions fuels, efficiency and electrification. Data-centre electricity demand rises from 485 TWh in 2025 to about 950 TWh in 2030 in the IEA central projection. More than 2,500 GW of generation, storage and large-load projects are already waiting in grid-connection queues. (IEA, 2026b; I

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 4 resources. The question is how quickly national infrastructure, institutions, human capital and industrial capability convert resource income into durable productive capacity. (IMF, 2026b; World Bank, 2026b) The core recommendation is to treat resource security as a system, not as a set of isolated commodities. Governments should map dependencies across the full stack, build strategic inventories where economics support them, diversify supply and processing, accelerate power and grid investment, protect open trade where possible, and anchor resource partnerships to local capability. Corporations should move from annual procurement logic to multi-year supply assurance, scenario testing, energy contracting, geographic redundancy and board-level dependency governance. Twelve numbers defining the new order Metric Strategic meaning US$3.4T IEA estimate of global energy investment in 2026. US$2.2T 2026 investment into low-emissions energy, grids, storage, efficiency and electrification. 950 TWh IEA central projection for data-centre electricity demand in 2030. 2,500+ GW Projects stalled in global grid-connection queues. 692 GW Renewable power capacity added in 2025. 72% Average share of the top refining country for key minerals excluding rare earths in 2025.
