THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 5 Figure 1-1. WTO modelled long-run effects under alternative trade-system scenarios. These are scenarios, not forecasts. A practical resource-security model therefore needs three filters. First, criticality: how much economic or security value depends on the input? Second, vulnerability: how concentrated is supply, how long is replacement lead time, and how limited are substitutes? Third, intervention efficiency: which tool reduces exposure at the lowest total economic cost? Strategic inventories fit short disruptions. Long-term offtake supports financing. Recycling reduces import dependence. Geographic diversification addresses single-country exposure. Grid investment solves an infrastructure constraint that stockpiles do not. This distinction is central to the thesis of this paper. Resource security is not synonymous with self-sufficiency. For most economies, full self-sufficiency is unrealistic and costly. Strategic resilience comes from diversified access, trusted partnerships, transparent markets, sufficient inventories, spare capacity where justified and infrastructure able to absorb shocks. CHAPTER 02 The 2026 Operating Environment War and technology are pushing the world economy in opposite directions at the same time. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ The global economy entered late 2026 under two large and opposing impulses. The Middle East conflict generated an adverse energy and shipping shock. At the same time, the AI investment cycle supported technology-related capital expenditure and trade. The IMF July 2026 update projected global growth of 3.0% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, with the negative energy shock partly offset by stronger technology activity. Global headline inflation was projected to rise

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 6 CHAPTER 03 Critical Minerals Become Strategic Infrastructure Small-volume inputs now support trillions of dollars of downstream economic activity. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Critical minerals sit at the intersection of clean energy, digital systems, advanced manufacturing, aerospace and defence. Their strategic role comes less from market size than from irreplaceability inside high-value products. A small disruption in gallium, germanium, graphite, magnet rare earths or tungsten carries consequences far beyond the revenue of the upstream market. The IEA 2026 outlook shows a broad tightening in strategic materials. Base-metal prices including copper rose sharply between January 2025 and April 2026. Lithium prices more than doubled from their prior trough, while cobalt prices rose about 130%, influenced by supply policy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Strategic minor minerals rose even faster in several cases as export controls tightened. (IEA, 2026a) Demand growth remains structural. UNCTAD projects lithium demand 353% higher in 2040 than in 2024 and graphite demand 131% higher. Clean technologies rise from 62% of lithium demand in 2024 to 87% by 2040. This does not imply a straight-line commodity supercycle. Technology substitution, recycling, project execution and demand uncertainty will produce cycles. The strategic point is that more economic systems depend on secure mineral access. (UNCTAD, 2026a) Figure 3-1. Selected upstream and refining concentration in 2025. Source: UNCTAD Global Trade Update, June 2026. Concentration differs by stage. Mining often reflects geology. Processing reflects industrial policy, energy cost, infrastructure, technical know-how, permitting and decades of investmen

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 7 Mineral / group Strategic demand Primary vulnerability Decision priority Gallium / germanium Semiconductors, optics, radar, electronics By-product dependence and concentrated processing Recovery from smelters, strategic inventories Tungsten Defence, tooling, high-temperature uses Concentrated supply and limited substitutes Diversification, stockpiles, recycling CHAPTER 04 Processing Is the Leverage Point The strategic contest is moving from reserves to refining, separation, smelting and component production. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Resource endowment is only the first layer of strategic power. Processing determines purity, specifications, qualification and access to downstream industries. A country with large reserves but limited refining capacity often exports lower-value material and imports higher-value products. A processing hub without dominant geology still captures industrial margin, technical capability, jobs and influence over customers. This is especially visible in rare earths. Mining diversification has progressed faster than separation, metal, alloy and permanent- magnet capacity. The IEA estimates roughly US$60 billion of investment over the next decade would support diversified magnet rare-earth supply chains outside the dominant supplier. The figure is modest against the annual downstream production exposed to a full disruption. (IEA, 2026a) Base-metal smelters also deserve renewed strategic attention. Several critical minor minerals are recovered as by-products of copper, zinc and lead processing. A modern smelter therefore functions as more than a producer of the headline metal. It becomes a recovery platform for strategic elements, a recycling hub and an anchor for downstream manufa

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 8 Figure 5-1. IEA central projection for data-centre electricity demand. Power density creates a second constraint. The IEA notes that advanced server racks are moving toward peak demands comparable with dozens of households per rack. AI server power density rose elevenfold between 2020 and 2025 and is expected to rise further by 2027. This places pressure on transformers, switchgear, power electronics and thermal-management systems. (IEA, 2026b) Storage is becoming part of the data-centre architecture. The IEA estimates 20 to 25 GW of battery storage could sit at data centres by 2030. Such assets support ride-through, power quality and flexible grid interaction. Where properly integrated, a large load shifts from passive consumer toward controllable system resource. (IEA, 2026b) Location economics therefore change. Land and tax incentives matter, yet power availability, connection speed, grid reliability, fibre connectivity, cooling conditions, regulatory approval and data sovereignty increasingly determine project viability. A jurisdiction with abundant cheap generation but weak transmission still loses. A jurisdiction with a strong grid but no incremental generation faces price pressure. A jurisdiction with power but weak digital and cyber governance faces another constraint. For resource-rich developing economies, AI infrastructure presents both opportunity and caution. Reliable low-cost electricity and political stability provide a basis for regional compute. Yet large data-centre loads should not crowd out households, industry or mining. Contracts need transparent cost allocation, new-generation commitments and grid investment obligations where appropriate. STRATEGIC LINK AI leadership is no long

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 9 Figure 6-1. Global grid queues and IEA estimate of capacity potentially released by reforms and grid-enhancing technologies. The IEA estimates annual grid investment needs to rise roughly 50% by 2030 from around US$400 billion today. A large share of the problem is execution: permitting, interconnection studies, transformer and cable lead times, right-of-way, financing and cost allocation. These are institutional and industrial bottlenecks as much as engineering issues. (IEA, 2026c) The near-term opportunity is not limited to building new lines. The IEA estimates that non-firm connection agreements, dynamic line rating, advanced power-flow controls, reconductoring, voltage upgrades and related reforms could release 1,200 to 1,600 GW of advanced-stage projects now waiting in queues. This is a material reminder that software, regulation and operating practices are part of infrastructure strategy. (IEA, 2026c) Grid equipment also has a mineral and manufacturing footprint. Transformers depend on electrical steel, copper and specialized components. Power electronics depend on semiconductors. Storage depends on battery materials. New transmission requires conductors, towers and civil works. Resource security therefore feeds back into the ability to build the electricity system needed to reduce fossil-fuel exposure. For boards and governments, the critical shift is to treat grid access as a strategic asset. Mining expansions, industrial parks, data centres, ports and processing plants should be screened against firm-power and interconnection timelines at the earliest investment stage. A nominal generation surplus does not equal deliverable power. CHAPTER 07 Energy Security Becomes Portfolio Security The 202

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 10 Figure 7-1. Global energy investment allocation in 2026. Source: IEA. The central strategic lesson is diversification. Domestic renewable resources reduce exposure to imported fuels. Gas provides dispatchable power in many systems but carries trade-route and price risk for importers. Nuclear offers firm low-carbon generation but depends on long project cycles, specialized technology and fuel-cycle supply. Storage provides short-duration flexibility but relies on mineral-intensive manufacturing. Efficiency lowers the amount of energy exposed to every supply shock. Renewables continue to scale. IRENA records 692 GW of renewable capacity additions in 2025, including 510 GW solar and 159 GW wind. Renewables represented 85.6% of global capacity additions and 49% of installed global power capacity at year-end. Deployment remains uneven: China, the United States and European Union together accounted for nearly four-fifths of additions. (IRENA, 2026) Figure 7-2. Renewable capacity additions in 2025. Source: IRENA. Nuclear is also returning to strategic planning. IEA reports 78 GW under construction across 15 countries and annual investment above US$80 billion. More than 40 countries have policies supporting nuclear deployment. The supply side is concentrated, with Chinese and Russian reactor designs representing a large share of projects that began construction over the prior decade. (IEA, 2026d) Portfolio security therefore requires a technology-neutral risk lens. The relevant question is which combination of domestic resources, imports, storage, networks and demand flexibility delivers acceptable reliability and price exposure under multiple stress cases. CHAPTER 08 Chokepoints and Trade Corridors Shippin

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 11 Modern value chains depend on narrow physical corridors. The Strait of Hormuz is the clearest 2026 example. UNCTAD estimates about one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade uses the route, alongside large shares of oil and LNG. When transit falls, the shock travels through freight, insurance, fuel, agriculture and consumer prices. (UNCTAD, 2026c) Figure 8-1. Approximate global trade exposure to the Strait of Hormuz before the 2026 disruption. The strategic response is not to eliminate maritime trade. Shipping remains the most efficient route for large volumes of commodities. The objective is to reduce single-corridor dependence where practical. Bypass pipelines, alternative ports, distributed storage, spare terminal capacity and diversified suppliers all carry option value during crisis. The same logic applies to minerals. A diversified mine base still depends on ports, rail, concentrate handling and refining routes. A smelter depends on imported feedstock, reagents, power and spare parts. A battery plant depends on chemical precursors, cells or components. Mapping chokepoints therefore needs to extend beyond country-of-origin statistics into physical logistics and industrial dependencies. Climate risk adds another layer. Drought can affect canal capacity and hydropower. Floods can halt mines and railways. Extreme heat raises power loads and affects labour productivity. Physical resilience and geopolitical resilience increasingly overlap. BOARD-LEVEL TEST For each critical input, leaders should know the mine or source, processor, transport corridor, port, inventory buffer, substitute, contract counterparty and recovery time. Country-of-origin alone is insufficient. CHAPTER 09 Trade Policy Become

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 12 Figure 9-1. WTO modelled GDP effects under alternative trading-system scenarios. The optimal policy is therefore selective. Protecting every sector under a security label would raise costs, weaken competition and invite retaliation. Strategic intervention should focus on inputs with high criticality, concentrated supply, low substitutability and long recovery time. Transparency around the rationale and duration of support reduces the risk of permanent protection becoming an end in itself. For developing economies, the new policy environment creates negotiating space. Resource partnerships increasingly cover exploration, extraction, processing, recycling and finance. Yet UNCTAD finds agreements involving developing states still tend to emphasize upstream extraction. The policy objective should shift toward infrastructure, skills, processing, technology transfer and market access alongside resource supply. (UNCTAD, 2026a) CHAPTER 10 Defence and Strategic Stockpiles Material security has moved from procurement into deterrence and national readiness. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Defence systems are material-intensive, specification-intensive and difficult to substitute once platforms enter service. Gallium, germanium, titanium, tungsten, graphite, cobalt, lithium and rare earths support radar, sensors, optics, aerospace alloys, batteries, motors and electronics. Supply disruption therefore affects readiness even when defence budgets rise. NATO has formalized this concern. Its defence-critical supply-chain roadmap identifies twelve critical raw-material categories and includes strategic stockpiling, recycling, substitution and shared supply-chain assessments. In July 2026, twelve Allies launched a multinationa

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 13 The composition matters. Grid spending is rising after years when generation investment expanded faster. Data-centre buildout is also drawing energy capital. The IEA estimates more than US$100 billion was invested in energy infrastructure serving data centres in 2025, including generation, power equipment, grid upgrades and onsite assets. (IEA, 2026d) Critical-mineral finance is more difficult. The IEA reports investment in critical-mineral development fell in 2025 even as strategic concern rose. Battery-metal spending declined more sharply than copper. This mismatch reflects weak commodity prices in prior periods, cost inflation, permitting, financing conditions and uncertainty about future demand and policy. Strategic need does not automatically produce bankable projects. Governments are responding with guarantees, state equity, offtake, price support, concessional finance and export-credit tools. Such instruments are most effective when they solve a defined financing gap rather than substitute public money for commercially viable private capital. Developing economies face an additional hurdle: cost of capital. A processing plant or grid project that is economic at a 6% financing rate may fail at 12%. Resource partnerships therefore need a finance architecture, not only an exploration agreement. Development banks, sovereign funds, export-credit agencies and strategic buyers all have roles in reducing risk around infrastructure that supports several projects at once. Capital problem Why private finance hesitates Useful de-risking tool New mine Price volatility, permitting, construction risk Long-term offtake, political-risk cover, staged financing Refinery / separator Feedstock and price risk, tech

IEA analysis finds the region processes only a fraction of its mined output for several key energy minerals. Greater local processing, where commercially supported, raises the value retained from mining and strengthens regional industrial capability. The IEA estimates deeper processing could lift the associated economic value toward roughly US$220 billion by 2035. (IEA, 2026a) Power quality is a decisive differentiator. Mineral processing, copper smelting, green metals, data centres and advanced manufacturing need large volumes of reliable electricity. Latin America has strong hydro, solar and wind potential, but grid constraints and permitting limit the value of theoretical resource abundance in several markets. Regional growth remains weak outside resource outliers. The World Bank October 2026 update projects Latin America and the Caribbean at 2.2% growth in 2026, while Guyana stands far above the regional average. This divergence creates a policy opportunity for fast-growing resource economies to finance infrastructure during a period when many regional peers face tighter fiscal conditions. (World Bank, 2026a) The region should avoid a binary choice between China and Western partners. Sector-specific multi-alignment, transparent investment standards and diversified buyers preserve bargaining space. The key is to prevent strategic partnerships from becoming exclusive dependencies at a different point in the chain. The values refer to different dates and are therefore not conflicting measures. They illustrate the speed at which resource revenues are changing the state's financial position. (IMF, 2026b; World Bank, 2026b) This creates a strategic choice. Guyana could remain principally a high-income hydrocarbon exporter with imported industrial capability, or use the resource window to build low-cost power, logistics, technical skills, digital systems, competitive non-oil sectors and stronger institutions. The second path is harder. It offers more resilience beyond the oil cycle. Energy is the first lever. The gas-to-energy program is intended to reduce reliance on imported liquid fuels in electricity generation and lower power costs. If delivered with transmission upgrades, storage and renewable integration, lower-cost electricity would support mining, manufacturing, cold-chain logistics, data services and household welfare. The strategic metric is not project completion alone, but delivered reliability and system cost. (IMF, 2026b) Mining is the second lever. Gold provides an existing ecosystem of geology, equipment, logistics, government regulation and international markets. The next step is not to force every downstream activity locally. The priority is to deepen technical services, responsible sourcing, digital traceability, environmental performance, exploration capability and local procurement around competitive operations. Logistics is the third lever.

THE NEW RESOURCE SECURITY ORDER RAGUNAUTH RAMSAROOP | OCTOBER 2026 | 16 CHAPTER 15 Corporate Strategy for 2026-2040 Resource security should sit inside enterprise risk, capital allocation and commercial strategy. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Most companies still manage strategic inputs through procurement, sustainability or operations teams. The emerging risk profile requires board-level integration. A mineral or power interruption can halt revenue across multiple business units, while a low-value component can disable a high-value asset. Traditional spend-based supplier rankings therefore miss criticality. The first step is a dependency map. For each business line, identify inputs whose failure would stop production, degrade safety or breach customer commitments. Trace each input beyond the direct supplier into processors, origin countries, logistics corridors, power dependencies and technology licenses. Measure recovery time, not only inventory days. The second step is a portfolio response. Inputs with short recovery times may need ordinary dual sourcing. Inputs with long qualification cycles may need multi-year offtake. Items with no substitutes may justify strategic inventory. Electricity-intensive operations may need long-term power contracts, onsite generation, storage or location diversification. The third step is capital discipline. Resilience spending should compete against expected disruption losses. Management should model revenue at risk, restart cost, reputational exposure, customer penalties and working-capital effects. This creates a common financial language for comparing inventory, supplier diversification and capital projects. The fourth step is policy engagement. Export controls, sanctions, tariffs, local-content requirements and national-security rules inc

New mines, lines, ports and processing facilities need land, permits and community acceptance. Faster execution does not mean weaker standards. Predictable timelines, transparent benefit sharing and early consultation reduce both project risk and political opposition. Governments and firms should select actions with value across several states of the world. Grid modernization, recycling, supplier transparency, workforce development, faster permitting and digital dependency mapping perform well in almost every scenario. Broad protectionism does not. Export controls, conflicts, grid bottlenecks and technology demand can move within months. Leadership teams should maintain a compact dashboard that links physical supply with market, policy and infrastructure signals. Finance determines how quickly alternatives reach commercial scale. Resource security is therefore a systems problem. The strongest strategies will target real chokepoints rather than pursue broad self-sufficiency. They will preserve cooperation where possible, build alternatives where necessary and keep public support tied to measurable resilience outcomes. For Guyana and other resource-rich emerging economies, the opportunity is larger than export revenue. The new order places a premium on reliable energy, strategic geography, minerals, governance and investment access. The long-term prize is not resource extraction. THE RESEARCH BRIEF From freshwater abundance to verifiable security. Guyana's water story is not scarcity in the abstract. It is the challenge of converting abundant freshwater into verifiably safe, reliable, affordable and climate-resilient service while protecting wetlands, rivers, aquifers and public health. 98.4%Administrative potable-water access Government, October 2025 [3] 67.2%Safely managed drinking water UN SDG country profile, 2024 [21] 77%Treated-water coverage at end-2025 Budget Speech 2026, printed p. 61 [5] What is new in this edition This publication edition integrates 10 original analytical exhibits, a traceable 38-source register, three reproducible economic and water-loss scenario families, source-precision notes, verification protocols and a specialist review dossier. It is independently authored document-based research, not a substitute for site investigations, engineering feasibility work or statutory approval. Executive summary Guyana is endowed with extensive rivers, high rainfall, forests, wetlands and groundwater. Historical interna- tional water accounts place internal renewable freshwater resources at approximately 241 cubic kilometres annually. Yet a national volume estimate does not describe what households receive, whether treatment works through the distribution network, how aquifers respond to abstraction, or whether drainage systems protect settled areas during extreme rainfall. Water security must be measured at the point of use and at the watershed scale, not inferred from total rainfall or river discharge. 1,2 Recent public investment has materially expanded access and treatment infrastructure. In October 2025, government reported that 98.4% of Guyana's population had access to potable water, including approximately 92% of people in hinterland and riverine areas. The definitions, sampling approaches and service conditions behind administrative access figures differ from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) definition of safely managed drinking water : an improved source on premises, available when needed, and free from faecal and priority chemical contamination. The figures should appear side by side, never as interchangeable measures. 3,4 The internationally comparable UN SDG country profile reports that 67.2% of Guyana's population used safely managed drinking water in 2024 and 43.4% used safely managed sanitation. It also reports 33.4% of domestic wastewater flows safely treated in 2024. These series are estimates for stated indicator definitions, not audits of each 2026 network. The 2024 UN water figure and the October 2025 national 98.4% administrative access figure must not be subtracted to produce an alleged service-quality failure rate. They h

The 2025 IDB financing programme is a concrete test of execution. A US$30 million conditional credit-line envelope, with a US$15.57 million first individual loan and separately identified US$36.33 million proposed JICA cofinancing, is intended to support a new Diamond plant, approximately 15 km of associated pipes, metering, leakage interventions and utility digitalisation. An estimated 151,560 people are prospective beneficiaries, not verified completed beneficiaries. The IDB project is listed as in implementation as of September 2026. Financing envelopes, individual loans and cofinancing are distinct accounting concepts and must not be added blindly. 22,23 This paper presents a 2026-2035 decision framework rather than an unsupported national cost estimate. It distinguishes verified results, historical indicators, announced targets, proposed technical options and unresolved data. Investment options cover network loss management, wastewater, aquifer monitoring, climate- resilient treatment and drainage, village water systems, source protection and common public reporting. A staged implementation scorecard specifies what should be measured before outcomes are claimed. Its overall objective is a national freshwater system whose quality, reliability, environmental performance and maintenance capacity can be independently checked. How to interpret and reproduce this paper The strongest evidence in a public water assessment is observed performance with an identified time, geo- graphy and denominator. A national access statement and a local treatment-plant pressure record may both be accurate, but the two answer different questions. National projections are particularly vulnerable to false precision when current withdrawal, loss and asset-registry data are missing. The analytical model supplied with this edition therefore varies a defined set of assumptions rather than presenting a single unsupported 2035 demand prediction. Exhibit 02. Conceptual basin-to-service map. A topological diagram of the four major Atlantic-draining systems and the coastal water- service overlay. It assigns no unverified catchment areas or annual flow shares. 2,29 1.1 Major river systems Guyana's four major Atlantic-draining river systems are the Essequibo, Demerara, Berbice and Corentyne. The Essequibo draws on substantial tributaries, including the Potaro, Mazaruni, Cuyuni and Rupununi. Southern boundary rivers such as the Takutu and Ireng connect Guyana hydrologically with the Amazon system through Brazil. The Corentyne is a transboundary waterway associated with Suriname. These river networks support transport, agriculture, fisheries, domestic water, forests, wetlands, settlements and commercial development. 2 Water flows across administrative boundaries. Upstream sediment loads, wastewater discharges or changed land cover alter downstream conditions. New intakes also compete with ecological flows, navigation, flood- plains and customary water uses. For this reason, the unit for managing source protection should include the drainage basin, sub-basin and aquifer system in addition to local government boundaries. 1.2 Coastal water management The low coastal plain contains most population centres and major areas of irrigated agriculture. Sea defences, drainage canals, kokers, pumps, conservancies and irrigation channels shape local water movement. During heavy rainfall, high tides or elevated river levels, gravity drainage becomes difficult. Saltwater intrusion becomes more consequential during low freshwater flow and prolonged dry periods. CDB identifies intense rainfall, groundwater contamination following floods, severe drought and saltwater intrusion as relevant hazards for water supply. 7 Infrastructure deci

1.3 Interior forests and wetland systems Interior catchments receive and retain rainfall through forests, soils, wetlands and floodplains. These ecosystems modify runoff, sediment movement, infiltration and dry-season ecological conditions. The North Rupununi wetlands are particularly important for freshwater biodiversity, community livelihoods, fish nurseries and seasonal floodplain connectivity. Published ecohydrological work reports exceptionally high fish diversity and habitats for arapaima, black caiman, giant river otters and river turtles. These biological observations do not substitute for current water-budget measurements; they establish the need to protect ecological flows and habitat connections when considering engineering changes. 9,10 1.4 A common interpretation error An estimate of approximately 241 km3 per year in internal renewable freshwater is a national accounting measure. It is not equivalent to daily dependable volume at Georgetown, an agricultural intake in Berbice, a village in the Pakaraimas or a particular mining catchment. Storage, treatment, river seasonality, groundwater recharge, water rights, contamination and energy availability affect local supply. The analysis therefore uses national endowment as context, not as evidence that any region is free of water risk. 1 2. Drinking-water coverage: access, quality and continuity Exhibit 04. Six non-equivalent service measures. Government 2025 administrative access and treatment results, UN 2024 household and wastewater estimates. The denominators, definitions and reference years differ. 3,5,20,21 2.1 Separating three different measures Administrative potable-water access records the population served under a national programme. Treated-water coverage records the reach of treatment. JMP safely man

community may appear in the first category and still lack household-level safely managed service if supply is intermittent, collection is distant, household storage is unsafe or distribution water is contaminated. Reporting should therefore publish all three measures without combining their denominators. 3,4 The October 2025 government access report gave 98.4% nationwide access and about 92% in hinterland and riverine communities. The January 2026 budget gave end-2025 treated-water coverage of 77%, up from 52% in 2020. Both statements can be true because they describe different indicators. 6. Agricultural water security and food-system resilience Agriculture requires dependable water at the right time, in the right location and at suitable salinity. Rice, sugar, livestock and diversified crops face different seasonal demand patterns and water-quality limits. Coastal conservancies and drainage channels often perform dual functions: retaining freshwater for agriculture while disposing of excess rainfall. Conflicting operating objectives must be identified explicitly in water-management rules. In an extended dry period, allocation should consider drinking water, ecological minimums, livestock and crops, industrial continuity and available storage. During extreme rainfall, pumping may protect one agricultural block while transferring peak flows downstream. A basin and drainage-district approach should therefore record intakes, flow control, conveyance losses, crop calendars and receiving-water impacts. Options include calibrated irrigation scheduling, field moisture monitoring, improved canal control, storage rehabilitation, water-user reporting and salinity alerts. Farmers need decisions based on local water levels and water-quality data rather than broad annual rainfall projections. Economics should include pumping energy, crop yield, lost days from waterlogging, salinity recovery and maintenance of canals and structures. Agricultural pollutants also require proportionate surveillance. Nutrient or pesticide sampling should reflect actual farming systems and application calendars. Risk controls may involve buffer strips, drainage timing, storage of agrochemicals, integrated pest management and targeted extension support. Such controls should be assessed against measured contamination and farmer adoption costs instead of blanket assumptions. 7. Industry, mini

8. Freshwater ecosystems and Indigenous stewardship Guyana's forests, rivers and wetlands deliver functions often omitted from engineering balance sheets. Riparian forests limit erosion and moderate localized sediment transfer. Wetlands store water, attenuate flood peaks under appropriate conditions and support fisheries and wildlife. Mangroves support coastal protection and biodiversity but do not eliminate the need for engineered sea defences or drainage management. Their actual hydrological contributions should be assessed site by site. 9,10 North Rupununi illustrates the connection among water, Indigenous livelihood systems and conservation. Seasonal inundation supports fisheries and habitat connectivity. Infrastructure projects must consider village knowledge, customary use, migration routes, fish breeding sites and the timing of floods. Community organisa- tions need meaningful participation in defining monitoring locations and interpreting local changes. 9 A conservation programme should report ecological condition in addition to area protected. Suitable indicators include wetland connectivity, water levels, seasonality, turbidity, habitat condition, fish assemblages where feasible and agreed livelihood outcomes. Restoration should avoid planting or engineered interventions that disrupt natural flood regimes. Funding models include government budgets, grant finance, ecosystem restora- tion projects and responsibly governed conservation programmes. Revenue estimates should not be presented as bankable without a defined methodology and market pathway. 9. 16. Implementation risk and institutional capacity Major delivery risks are not confined to construction. They include poor source data, unmetered assets, unsuitable technology selection, unreliable power, lack of skilled operators, delayed spare parts, inadequate laboratory coverage, overlapping institutional mandates and insufficient recurrent funding. Land, environmental and community-consent processes may also alter schedules. These risks should be visible in public project appraisal rather than hidden within contingency percentages. Water projects need clear acceptance gates. Engineering completion should lead to commissioning tests, then a defined reliability trial, then ordinary operating performance reporting. Financial closeout should be tied to the availability of as-built drawings, operating manuals, parts lists, asset-register updates, water-safety plans and trained operators. Independent verification is especially valuable for large facilities whose output will affect multiple downstream communities. For remote infrastructure, a maintenance agreement should name the entity accountable for pump failures, the maximum replacement lead time and the budget source. For large utilities, a common asset-management system should connect work orders, failures, metering, energy use and costs. For environmental monitoring, independent laboratories and consistent chain-of-custody arrangements improve confidence without displacing regulator authority. 17. Appendix B. Core calculation definitions Non-revenue water: NRW (%) = (system input volume - billed authorized consumption) / system input volume x 100. The calculation should account transparently for authorised unbilled consumption and differences between bulk-meter and customer-meter periods. The percentage alone does not identify physical leakage. Treatment capacity factor: Actual annual treated volume / (rated MLD x actual calendar operating days). The denominator must distinguish design nameplate capacity from permitted or seasonally derated capacity. Report water meeting standards separately from gross throughput. Water balance at an industrial site: Opening storage + freshwater intake + rainfall capture + recycled inflow - evaporation - product incorporation - discharge - other losses = closing storage, within documented measurement error. Water recycled internally must not be double-counted as new withdrawal. Groundwater response: Track static and pumping heads in representative observation wells with clear elevation datum, rainfall and pumping context. A one-time falling head cannot establish an irreversible aquifer decline or saltwater intrusion. Wastewater effectiveness: Report the volume entering treatment, volume leaving treatment, proportion meet- ing permit standards and bypass volume. Treatment-plant capacity is not a proxy for pollutant removal or environmental compliance. Climate resilience: State the hazard combination, return-period or scenario assumptions where applicable, local land elevation datum, critical equipment protection level, power redundancy and post-event recovery objective. D.1 National sampling logic Sampling must distinguish dry and wet periods, upstream reference locations and downstream compliance stations, household taps and treatment outlets, and shallow versus confined aquifer horizons. A statistically designed household survey should stratify coastal/hinterland areas and service types, then weight results to an explicitly dated population frame. Testing only plants that voluntarily supply data or communities reached easily by road would not establish national service quality. For mine-related mercury, turbidity or metal concerns, establish site-specific potential pathways before selecting samples. A single high suspended-sediment reading does not establish elevated methylmercury in fish. Fish-tissue surveillance requires species and size controls, consumption information, laboratory quality assurance and human exposure interpretation by qualified practitioners. Avoid extrapolating any single mining district's results across all inland water bodies. D.2 Publication-ready audit controls Each factual table and figure should have a versioned source and extraction note, a definition of its population or denominator, a quality category and a reviewer field. Every quantitative forecast should be reproducible from parameter values, formulae and scenario labels. Where official sources conflict, publish both statements, identify why they may differ, and record the follow-up request rather than selecting the larger or more politically convenient number. Citation URLs should be checked before each new digital edition. The source- audit CSV supplied with this package is a starter ledger, not an institutional audit certificate. Appendix F. Calculation audit and reproducibility F.1 Demand model: Billed authorised demand (MLD) = assumed served population (millions) x assumed billed L/ person/day. Required system input (MLD) = billed authorised demand / (1 - NRW). This simplified model excludes authorised unbilled use, storage changes, fire demand, industrial demand and seasonal peaking. The companion CSV contains 36 scenario combinations. The population series are assumptions, not the 2022 census or an approved 2035 population forecast. F.2 Loss scenarios: Annual volume of independently measured real water saved (m³) = sustained real savings in MLD x 1,000 x 365. Commercial loss improvement creates accounting and revenue benefits, but is not automatically physically recovered water. F.3 Plant-capital analogue: GYD 1.3bn / 12 MLD = GYD 108.33m per installed MLD for a particular announced 2025 plant. Ten notional MLD at half, one and twice this quotient gives GYD 0.542bn, 1.083bn and 2.167bn initial capex. These are scenario outputs, not local tenders or site designs. F.4 Discounted operating exposure: At 6% real discount, 20 equal year-end payments have factor (1 - 1.06^-20)/0.06 = 11.4699. Annual O&M scenario = initial capital x 3%, 5% or 8%; discounted operating present value = annual O&M x annuity factor. Environmental mitigation, periodic overhaul, distribution mains, financing charges and residual values are excluded from this deliberately narrow illustration. F.5 Traceability: Every calculated table is reproducible from the files in the publication packet. Numerical outputs should be recalculated if an input source is corrected. The model is intended to demonstrate how missing local data alter public-investment choices, not to substitute for a feasibility study. RR / INDEPENDENT RESEARCH GU
